All SRS imagery and their derived spectral and textural features used in this study are summarized in Table 1, corresponding to the 22 predictor variables used as inputs for the biomass prediction model. All images were reprojected to the EPSG:3857 (Pseudo-Mercator) coordinate system to ensure tile alignment across datasets.
Land cover data

WorldCover, produced by the European Space Agency (ESA), is a 10-meter resolution land cover dataset available for the years 2020 and 2021. The product was generated using Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, in combination with the Copernicus Global 30 m DEM and various auxiliary datasets, through a gradient-boosted decision tree classifier. WorldCover achieves a global overall accuracy of 74.4% and is publicly accessible at https://esa-worldcover.org. In this study, we used the 2020 WorldCover land cover product as a base map to mask and extract China's major vegetation types, including forests, croplands, grasslands, shrublands, and wetlands, for biomass estimation and reporting.
AGB estimation

Given the horizontal geolocation uncertainty of +-10 meters at the center of each GEDI footprint, directly aligning GEDI data with SRS imagery can introduce spatial mismatches. To mitigate this issue, all input datasets (GEDI, SRS, and land cover data) were resampled to a common spatial resolution of 30 meters within GEE. This approach also helps reduce noise and contributes to improved performance of the machine learning models. Bilinear resampling was applied to the continuous GEDI and SRS data, while majority resampling was used for the categorical land cover data.

We employed the RF regression model on the GEE platform to extrapolate the discrete GEDI observations into spatially continuous AGBD estimates. Numerous studies have demonstrated that, compared with other commonly used regression models such as support vector machines and artificial neural networks, RF performs better in handling high-dimensional data. It is capable of modeling large numbers of non-independent or non-linearly separable predictor variables and is less sensitive to noise and feature selection. These properties make RF particularly well suited for monitoring complex ecosystems using diverse remote sensing variables, including forest height, biomass estimation, and forest classification.

In our regression model, 22 predictor variables (listed in Table 1) derived from Sentinel, PALSAR, and DEM datasets were used as input features, while GEDI AGBD values served as the predicted variable. A total of 54,393,995 GEDI observations across China were stratified and randomly split into a training dataset (70%) and a holdout testing dataset (30%) based on AGBD value distributions. The parameter numberOfTrees refers to the number of decision trees, while bagFraction defines the fraction of training samples randomly selected for building each decision tree (with the remaining samples left out for out-of-bag validation). We used an iterative search method to identify the optimal parameter combination. Specifically, the numberOfTrees was varied from 10 to 150 in steps of 10, and bagFraction from 0.1 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1. To improve computational efficiency and generalization performance, the optimal model configuration:defined by the highest prediction accuracy:was found to be numberOfTrees = 50 and bagFraction = 0.6.

Overview of the 508 geographical tiles used for local adaptive modeling. Seven blue rectangular tiles indicate selected representative vegetation regions for subsequent model performance evaluation: (a) Central Tibetan Plateau: Grasslands are the dominant vegetation type. (b) Northwestern Yunnan Province: A mosaic of croplands, forests, shrubs, and grasslands. (c) Southern Shaanxi Province: Dominated by croplands and forests. (d) Hainan Province: Forests are the main vegetation cover. (e) Central Inner Mongolia: Primarily composed of grasslands and croplands. (f) Hebei and Beijing regions: Transitional zones of croplands, forests, and grasslands. (g) Western Heilongjiang Province: Characterized mainly by croplands and the Zhalong Wetland.

Due to the enormous volume of remote sensing data at fine spatial resolution across a vast area, training a global RF model is computationally intensive and time-consuming. Moreover, the GEE platform imposes certain limitations in terms of processing capacity and memory usage. To balance prediction accuracy and computational efficiency, we adopted a locally adaptive regression approach. Specifically, China was divided into 508 geographic tiles (Fig. 2) and an independent RF model was trained within each tile to generate the national AGB map.

To reduce noticeable boundary effects, where AGB values predicted by different RF models may vary significantly at tile edges, we implemented a neighborhood-based training strategy. For each tile, the RF model was trained using samples from a 3 x 3 surrounding tile window, and predictions were generated for the center tile only.

Spatial and temporal dependencies within the training and validation datasets may lead to overestimation of model accuracy. To account for such dependencies and assess the extent to which each model generalizes to new data, we employed five-fold cross-validation. For each tile, we calculated the standard deviation (SD) of the root mean square error (RMSE) across multiple training-testing splits as a measure of overall model uncertainty. In addition, model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), RMSE and relative root mean square error (rRMSE), all computed based on the mean values from the validation datasets.Where n represents the sample size, , , and  represent the estimated AGB, observed AGB, and the average of observed AGB, respectively.
Evaluation of the model: predicted AGB from our model against AGB derived from GEDI.

In this study, model validation was performed using 30% of the in situ GEDI measurements. Gaussian kernel density estimation was applied to visualize the density of scatter points. The prediction model achieved an average R2 of 0.85, RMSE of 31.26 Mg/ha and rRMSE of 50.04% (Fig. 3(a)). In addition, the average SD across 5-fold cross-validation was 6.28 Mg/ha. Validation results for the locally adaptive RF models in seven representative regions are shown in Fig. 3(b-h). Across all 508 tiles, the R2, RMSE, rRMSE and SD ranged from 0.72 to 0.93, 5.72 to 59.90 Mg/ha, 25.47% to 85.69%, and 0.74 to 15.78 Mg/ha, respectively. These statistics indicate a strong correlation between the estimated AGBD and the GEDI observations, suggesting that the RF model generalizes well to new data. However, it tends to slightly overestimate low biomass and underestimate high biomass values. This tendency can be attributed to potential design bias in GEDI's model-based predictions, as discussed by Stahl et al.. They show that even high-quality remote sensing predictions can exhibit systematic biases due to limitations in the model training data, especially in regions where the model was trained with sparse or unbalanced field data.
Variable importance ranking based on Gini index.

Predictor variables were ranked based on Gini importance. Figure 4 illustrates their relative contributions to AGB estimation within the RF model. Variables derived from the GLO-30 DEM were more influential than those from other data sources. Specifically, four variables related to the red spectral band (B4, NDVI, BSI, and EVI) were the most important predictors, collectively contributing 17.02% to the model. Two topographic variables contributed the second highest share (15.81%), followed closely by SAR-based variables, which accounted for 15.80%.
Prediction map of AGB and relative RMSE map at 30 m resolution across China in 2020.

Figure 5(a) presents the predicted AGB map of China at a 30-meter resolution for the year 2020. A corresponding relative uncertainty map (Fig. 5(b)) was generated by calculating the ratio of the model's RMSE to the predicted AGB values. As shown in Fig. 5(a), AGB in China exhibits a clear increasing trend from the arid desert and steppe regions of the northwest to the forested areas of southeastern Tibet. The highest AGB values are concentrated in the tropical and monsoonal forests of southeastern Tibet, while the lowest values are found in the inland regions dominated by desert and semi-arid climates. Across the country, AGB values range up to 620.46 Mg/ha, with a national average of 44.03 Mg/ha. AGB uncertainty reaches a maximum of 59.90 Mg/ha, with a mean of 19.42 Mg/ha. Regions with relatively high uncertainty are primarily located in central and northern Inner Mongolia and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. The relative uncertainty map shows a generally negative correlation with AGB, indicating that areas with lower biomass tend to exhibit higher relative uncertainty.

Using the conversion factor of 0.47 between AGB and carbon stock, the total AGB storage across China's vegetated areas:including croplands, forests, grasslands, shrublands, and wetlands:was estimated at 20.20 Pg, with a national mean of 44.03 Mg/ha. Among these vegetation types, forests accounted for the largest share of AGB, totaling 13.50 Pg with an average of 119.36 Mg/ha, followed by grasslands (3.71 Pg; 36.34 Mg/ha), croplands (2.88 Pg; 40.92 Mg/ha), wetlands (0.06 Pg; 60.97 Mg/ha), and shrublands (0.04 Pg; 42.13 Mg/ha).
Data Records

This all-vegetation-type biomass product integrates multi-source remote sensing data acquired in 2020, including GEDI, Sentinel-2, PALSAR, WorldCover, and the GLO-30 DEM. As a result, it represents a temporally consistent biomass map for the year 2020. The dataset is freely available from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center via 10.11888/Terre.tpdc.302797. It is provided as GeoTIFF files at a spatial resolution of 30 meters, with AGB values expressed in units of megagrams per hectare (Mg/ha).
Technical Validation

Due to the limited availability of field-based biomass measurements that are temporally consistent with 2020 (most publicly available field datasets are concentrated between 2010 and 2015 or from other years), we adopted the following strategies to validate the biomass dataset presented in this study:
Comparison to existing forest AGB maps

To comprehensively assess the spatial patterns of the predicted AGB values, we compared our forest AGB estimates at the pixel level with three existing forest AGB products. These comparison datasets were selected based on temporal proximity (around the year 2020) or similar spatial resolution ( >=100 m). The selected products include: (1) a global forest AGB map for 2010 developed by Santoro et al., which integrates high-resolution satellite remote sensing data including ICESat/GLAS LiDAR, Sentinel-1, Envisat ASAR along with 110,897 field measurements; (2) a 30-meter resolution forest AGB map of China for 2019 produced by Guo and Yang et al., based on over 4,700 nationwide field plots and incorporating canopy height products, multispectral imagery, and environmental variables using a RF model; and (3) a product by He and Zhang et al., which estimates forest AGB across China from 2013 to 2020 by integrating high-resolution satellite data (e.g., the Gaofen series, Landsat, Sentinel) with forest assessment indicators under the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) framework.

To ensure comparability among the four AGB maps, we reprojected and resampled the three external products to match the projection and spatial resolution of our dataset using nearest-neighbor resampling. These harmonized datasets were then used to analyze differences in spatial distribution patterns and total forest carbon stocks across China.
Spatial distribution of forest AGB across China.

We masked and compared the estimated forest AGB from our study with other forest AGB maps, revealing broadly similar spatial patterns but also some notable differences (Fig. 6). Across all four maps, high AGB values are consistently concentrated in southern Tibet and the Sichuan-Yunnan region, while lower values dominate northern and central China. Additionally, our AGB map displays some high values in Taiwan, whereas the Guo map shows high biomass in northeastern China, and the He map highlights high values in Hainan. These spatial patterns are not present in the CCI map.
Frequency Distributions of AGB maps.

We further examined the histogram distributions of forest AGB values across the four maps (Fig. 7). The histogram derived from our study most closely resembles a normal distribution, and the majority of forest AGB values across all maps fall within the range of 50-150 Mg/ha. The CCI map displays a substantial proportion of low AGB values in the 0-30 Mg/ha range, which deviates significantly from the others. This discrepancy may reflect methodological differences among the products, such as the lower spatial resolution, forest masking criteria, the temporal mismatch with the 2010 reference year, or potential local deviations as a global dataset. The peak frequency of our distribution aligns most closely with the He map, both centered around 100-120 Mg/ha. In terms of variability, our map has a standard deviation similar to those of the CCI and He maps, while the Guo map shows the smallest SD at 31.67 Mg/ha.

Some of the differences in mean AGB and total carbon stock shown in Table 2 are primarily attributable to variations in the total forest area used in the calculations. These differences arise from divergent definitions of forests, which can significantly affect carbon stock estimates. According to the China Forestry and Grassland Statistical Yearbook, the national forest area was reported as 218 million hectares in 2020. In our study, non-forest areas were masked using the ESA WorldCover land cover product. The He map used a forest cover layer generated within their research, while the Guo map employed the Globeland30 forest cover product. These three maps have relatively similar forest area estimates, with the Guo map being the closest to the official statistical yearbook. In contrast, the CCI map utilized the Hansen global forest dataset for forest masking, which resulted in a significantly different forest area. Moreover, the CCI product reports carbon stocks for the year 2010, making it temporally inconsistent with the other datasets. Total aboveground carbon stock for China's forests was estimated by summing the carbon content of all forest pixels in each AGB map. Our study estimated China's total forest aboveground carbon stock at 13.50 Pg C, which is approximately 2.27 times higher than the value from the CCI map, and about 15% higher than the estimates from the Guo and He maps (Table 2).
Validation using field data
Spatial distribution of field data collected in 2020, 2023 and 2024, along with data from the Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC).

To evaluate the accuracy and applicability of the AGB map produced in this study, we collected field survey data from 78 forest plots in Sichuan Province (Fig. 8). These include five 667 m2 plots surveyed in 2020, twenty-two 400 m2 plots from 2023, and fifty-one 400 m2 plots from 2024. The plots were established using RTK-based positioning, with a preference for monospecific or relatively homogeneous stands. Tree height (H) and diameter at breast height (DBH) were measured within each plot, and the average AGB was calculated to serve as ground-truth data (see Eqs. 10,11) for comparison with the satellite-derived biomass estimates. To ensure temporal consistency between the ground samples and the biomass product, we also generated biomass maps for Sichuan Province for the years 2023 and 2024.Where , and  denote the aboveground biomass, standing volume per unit area, basic wood density, biomass expansion factor, plot area, and stem density for tree species j, respectively;  represents the allometric equation relating DBH and H to the aboveground biomass of an individual tree (whole-tree) for species j.

In addition, we extracted 76 observation records from 2020, spanning various months (mainly from May to October) across nine monitoring stations referenced in three previous studies, using data available from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC). These include two grassland ecosystem stations (Haibei and Inner Mongolia) and five desert ecosystem stations (Ordos, Fukang, Linze, Naiman, and Shapotou) used by Guo et al. for observations in China's arid and semi-arid regions. Additional records include AGB measurements at different phenological stages for soybean and millet at the Ansai station from Wang et al., and seasonal AGB data from fenced plots at different slope positions in the Yinshan Mountains foothills reported by Yao et al.. As the AGB values produced in this study represent annual mean aboveground biomass density, we calculated the annual mean AGB for each of the nine stations based on multiple monthly observations. These averaged values were then georeferenced and used as independent validation points against our biomass map.
Assessment of AGB map against independent field data.

The estimated AGB showed strong agreement with field-measured AGB at the pixel level. For the forest plots in Sichuan Province, the R2 and RMSE were 0.76 and 43.22 Mg/ha, respectively (Fig. 9(a)). For the grassland and cropland plots obtained from the TPDC, the R2 and RMSE were 0.50 and 9.33 Mg/ha, respectively (Fig. 9(b)). These results indicate that the model performs better in high-biomass forests than in low-biomass vegetation types. One contributing factor is the data preprocessing step, in which GEDI measurements with RSE greater than 50% were removed. This led to an underrepresentation of low AGB samples (e.g., <6 Mg/ha), which may have resulted in overestimation in low-biomass regions.

It is important to acknowledge the uncertainties associated with validation using the above field samples. First, the number of available ground-truth samples for grasslands, croplands, and shrublands was limited and not representative at the national scale. Second, there is a spatial resolution mismatch between our AGB map and the field plots, which could lead to geolocation discrepancies and imperfect spatial alignment. Therefore, establishing a more comprehensive and standardized vegetation observation network, along with developing biomass maps at higher spatial resolution, should be key priorities for future research.
Comparison with statistical yearbook 2020

Forest inventory data from the China Forestry and Grassland Statistical Yearbook 2020 were also used to validate the accuracy of estimated biomass at the national scale. The statistical report provides provincial-level data on forest area and growing stock. Guo et al. documented a method for converting stock volume density to AGBD at the provincial scale, as described in Eq. (12). Using this equation, we converted the reported stock volume for each province into AGB, enabling a comparative assessment of the accuracy of our provincial AGB estimates.where BD and VD are forest AGB (Mg/ha) and stock volume density (m3/ha), respectively.
Assessment of AGB maps against province-level statistical AGB.

Additionally, we compared the average AGB values across 32 first-level administrative regions in China (excluding Hong Kong and Macao) as derived from the yearbook and forest biomass products. The results are shown in Fig. 10. Our AGB product demonstrates a strong agreement with the yearbook-based estimates across the 32 regions (R2 = 0.78, RMSE = 22.22 Mg/ha; Fig. 10(a)). Compared to the statistical data, our estimates are higher in 25 provinces and lower in 7 provinces. Notably, the absolute errors in Ningxia and Hubei provinces exceed 30 Mg/ha. The AGB estimates from Guo's map also show good agreement with the statistical data (R2 = 0.74), with an RMSE that is 0.87 Mg/ha lower than that of our product. In contrast, the He map (R2 = 0.48) and the CCI map (R2 = 0.47) exhibit weaker correlations with the statistical data. In particular, the AGB values estimated by the CCI product are consistently below the 1:1 reference line (Fig. 10(b)), indicating a systematic underestimation compared to the yearbook reference values.

Based on the evaluation using field measurements and comparisons with statistical data and existing AGB maps, we propose that this new dataset represents a reliable estimate of China's total carbon stock and its spatial distribution for the year 2020. It can inform forest and grassland management decisions and support national carbon accounting efforts. The proposed modeling framework addresses key gaps in current approaches and can be extended to produce annual, wall-to-wall AGB maps at a 30-meter resolution for other regions, potentially at the global scale. While several previous studies have developed separate models for different plant functional types or land cover classes, our findings demonstrate that a unified model trained across multiple vegetation types is feasible. This approach reduces training time and effectively mitigates the accuracy loss associated with limited training samples in specific categories.
Usage Notes

The dataset presented in this study is publicly available for free download. It is worth noting that the modeling approach involved dividing the entire territory of China into 508 grid cells, within which locally adaptive models were trained. This grid-based partitioning may have segmented ecologically or climatically similar regions into separate training zones, potentially introducing slight boundary effects in transitional areas between adjacent tiles. Future work could improve the spatiotemporal consistency of AGB estimates in these transition zones by training local models based on ecological regions, vegetation zones, or administrative boundaries such as provinces. Additionally, GEDI L4A AGBD outputs can exhibit regional biases, particularly in areas like Asia where few calibration plots were used to train the L4A model. Users with access to more field inventory data from specific regions of interest could apply a local calibration curve for pre-training calibration, which helps reduce the propagation of residual design bias from the L4A inputs into the model, thereby improving the accuracy of biomass estimates. Finally, when applying this map to ecological modeling or carbon accounting in non-forest areas, users should fully account for the limitations associated with higher prediction uncertainty in low-biomass ecosystems, such as grasslands, shrublands, and croplands, due to the sparsity of field validation plots. Future efforts should focus on increasing field measurements in low-biomass regions to strengthen model calibration and validation.

passages.text: Integrated multi-omics reveals the molecular basis of protein storage in developing oat grains
Background

Oats (Avena sativa L.) are a nutritionally important cereal crop, but the molecular mechanisms regulating protein and amino acid accumulation during grain development remain poorly understood. Therefore, in this study, two oat varieties (HZ and MC) with significantly different grain protein contents were used as experimental materials. For the grains of these two varieties at different developmental stages, we conducted grain protein content determination, widely targeted metabolite detection, and transcriptome sequencing.
Results

Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses of two oat varieties (high-protein HZ and low-protein MC) revealed dynamic changes during grain filling. Key findings include: (1) The 10-20 days after flowering (DAF) period was critical for protein accumulation, with HZ showing higher expression of genes involved in carbon skeleton generation (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase) and amino acid biosynthesis (e.g., glutamate decarboxylase); (2) Weighted gene coexpression network analysis identified modules strongly correlated with protein content, including the blue module (r = 0.92, p < 0.01); (3) KEGG enrichment highlighted central roles for glycolysis, TCA cycle, and amino acid metabolism pathways; (4) A regulatory network for protein and amino acid accumulation was constructed, identifying 157 candidate genes and 7 metabolites. Four key genes (GLA, PFK, PGK, TIM) and a transcription factor (AP2/ERF-ERF ) were identified as critical regulators; (5) qRT-PCR validated 10 candidate genes, with expression patterns consistent with RNA-Seq data (R2 = 0.72-0.85).
Conclusions
This study elucidates the metabolic and transcriptional networks underlying protein accumulation in oat grains, providing targets for molecular breeding to enhance nutritional quality.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12870-025-07624-1.
Background

Oat (Avena sativa L.) is a globally significant gramineous crop, originating from the Middle East (e.g., Iran, Iraq, Syria, and Turkey) and the Iberian Peninsula. Oats are nutrient-dense, containing high levels of proteins (12-20%, three times that of rice), starches, and fats (over 5%, four times that of wheat). Unlike other cereals that primarily use prolamin as their storage protein, oats utilize globulin, which provides a balanced amino acid profile beneficial for human digestion. This makes oats less allergenic and more suitable for individuals with legume protein allergies. Consequently, oats hold potential as a functional ingredient in food processing. Protein quality is determined by amino acid composition, particularly the content and bioavailability of essential amino acids, which are vital for human growth, reproduction, and maintenance. Oats exhibit a superior amino acid profile compared to staple crops like rice and wheat, making them an excellent amino acid source. Seed development, a complex process involving changes in seed size and nutrient accumulation, directly influences crop yield and quality. Previous studies have attempted to enhance protein and amino acid content in cereal seeds through increased nitrogen fertilization. However, excessive nitrogen use can lead to soil acidification and biodiversity loss in aquatic ecosystems, posing environmental sustainability challenges. Thus, understanding the intrinsic biosynthesis mechanisms of grain proteins and amino acids is essential. Research has shown that transcription factors such as MADS-box, MYC, and NAC positively regulate grain storage protein content. In contrast, amino acid transporter family genes (CaAATs) may negatively regulate essential and non-essential amino acid levels in chickpeas. The amino acid transporter gene TaATLa1 facilitates the transport of glutamine, glutamate, and aspartate in yeast. Overexpression of TaATLa1 in Arabidopsis thaliana significantly increases leaf amino acid content and seed protein content, while its knockout in wheat disrupts amino acid transport and inhibits growth, demonstrating its role in amino acid source-sink transport in wheat. Similarly, overexpression of GmCGS2, a gene in the methionine synthesis pathway in soybeans, enhances methionine and free amino acid content in seeds. Despite these advances, the regulatory mechanisms underlying protein and amino acid synthesis during oat grain development remain poorly understood. This study investigated two oat varieties with distinct grain protein contents. Protein and amino acid levels were compared across different grain development stages. Using transcriptomic and widely targeted metabolomic datasets, the regulatory network governing protein and amino acid accumulation during oat grain development was analyzed, focusing on gene expression and metabolite dynamics. The findings aim to provide a theoretical foundation for improving oat quality and advancing molecular breeding strategies.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and sample preparation

The oat varieties used in this study, HZ (high protein) and MC (low protein), were provided by the Oat Genetic Breeding Research Group of Inner Mongolia Agricultural University. Both varieties were cultivated in 2023 at the Modern Agricultural Science and Technology Park of Inner Mongolia Agricultural University, located in Saihan District, Hohhot City, Inner Mongolia (111.87 E, 40.68 N). Plants with spikelets emerging on the same day were tagged after heading. Grain samples (approximately 10 g) were collected from tagged spikes at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 days after flowering (DAF), labeled as MC5, MC10, MC15, MC20, MC25, MC30, HZ5, HZ10, HZ15, HZ20, HZ25, and HZ30. After treat-ment with liquid nitrogen for 2 h, the samples were stored at -80  C. Three biological replicates were prepared for each sample, resulting in a total of 36 samples from 2 varieties across 6 developmental stages. Metabolic profiling and transcriptome sequencing were performed by Wuhan MetWare Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (www.metware.cn).
Determination of protein content

The grains used for the assay were dried seeds harvested at 30 days after flowering (30 DAF). These seeds were ground into a powder using a grinding mill and passed through an 80-mesh sieve to ensure sample homogeneity. An accurately weighed amount (0.2 g) of the well-mixed powder was transferred into a digestion tube, followed by the addition of 0.4 g of copper sulfate (CuSO4), 6 g of potassium sulfate (K2SO4), and 20 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4). The mixture was digested in a digestion furnace at 420  C for 1 h until the liquid in the tube turned into a clear, transparent blue-green color. After thorough cooling, the protein content of all 36 oat grain samples was determined using a fully automatic Kjeldahl nitrogen analyzer (KN680, Jinan Alva Instrument Co., Ltd.).
Metabolite extraction and UPLC-MS/MS analysis

Metabolite extraction was performed on 6 groups (18 samples in total) of oat grain samples from the HZ and MC varieties at three developmental stages (10, 20, and 30 DAF). After vacuum freeze-drying, the samples were ground into powder. Exactly 0.0500 g of powder was weighed and transferred to a 1.5 mL centrifuge tube, followed by the addition of 1200microL of 70% methanol solution pre-cooled to -20  C. The samples were vortexed every 30 min for a total of 6 times. After centrifugation at 1200 rpm for 3 min, the supernatant was collected, filtered through a 0.22 mum microporous membrane, and stored in sample vials for UPLC-MS/MS analysis. Data acquisition was conducted using Ultra Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) (ExionLC  AD, https://sciex.com.cn/) coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). Mass spectrometry data were processed using Analyst 1.6.3 to generate Total Ion Current (TIC) chromatograms for quality control (QC) samples and Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) extracted ion chromatograms (XIC). Metabolite content data were normalized using Z-score normalization in R software (www.r-project.org). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to assess sample separation trends. Pearson's Correlation Coefficient (r) was used to evaluate biological reproducibility. Heatmaps were generated using the Complex-Heatmap package in R for hierarchical clustering analysis of metabolite accumulation patterns. Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) values were calculated using the Orthogonal Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) model. Significantly differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs) were identified based on VIP > 1 and fold change (FC) 2 (up-regulated) or 0.5 (down-regulated). The DAMs were assigned to the KEGG Pathway database. A P -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Transcriptome sequencing and data analysis

To account for the lag between gene expression and metabolite synthesis, transcriptome sequencing was performed on 12 sample groups (36 samples in total), including additional samples at 5, 15, and 25 DAF. Total RNA was extracted using the modified Trizol method. mRNA with poly A tails was enriched using Oligo(dT) magnetic beads, fragmented, and reverse-transcribed into cDNA. Double-stranded cDNA was purified, end-repaired, A-tailed, and ligated with sequencing adapters. Size selection and PCR amplification were performed to construct cDNA libraries. Library quality was assessed, and qualified libraries were sequenced on the Illumina platform. Raw sequencing data were quality-controlled by removing adapter sequences, reads with > 5% undetermined bases, and low quality reads (more than 50% of bases with quality score Q 20). Clean reads were aligned to the reference genome (pepsico-oat-ot3098-v2-files-2021) using HISAT2. Gene expression levels were quantified as FPKM (Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per Million fragments mapped). Pearson correlation analysis and PCA were conducted to evaluate biological reproducibility and sample separation trends. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between developmental stages and varieties. DEGs were screened using log2 Fold Change 1 and FDR 0.05. Functional annotation and enrichment analysis were conducted using Gene On-tology and KEGG Pathway.
Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA)

The varFilter function in the R genefilter package was used to filter low-expression genes (FPKM < 1) and genes with constant expression levels. Coexpression network modules were constructed using the WGCNA package in R. The correlation coefficient was weighted to ensure a scale-free network distribution. The optimal soft threshold (beta-value) was determined using the pick-SoftThreshold function. Modules were clustered based on gene expression correlations, and highly correlated genes were grouped into modules. Modules were correlated with protein and amino acid content from metabolome data. The module with the highest correlation to protein content was selected for functional annotation and enrichment analysis.
Validation of candidate genes by real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR)

To validate transcriptome results, 10 DEGs with high expression levels and significant KEGG Pathway enrichment were selected for qRT-PCR. Primers were designed using Primer 3 Plus (https://www.primer3plus.com) based on CDS sequences of the selected DEGs and the reference gene (ACT). All primers were synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (Table S1).

Total RNA was extracted from approximately 0.1 g of oat seeds using the RNAprep Pure Plant Kit (Tiangen, Tianjin, China). RNA integrity was assessed by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis, while concentration and purity were measured using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer. First-strand cDNA synthesis was performed with the TIANGEN  FastKing cDNA First Strand Synthesis Kit. The reaction mixture consisted of 2 microL RNA, 2 microL 5x gDNA Buffer, 6 microL RNase-Free ddH2O, 2 microL 10x King RT Buffer, 1 microL FastKing RT Enzyme Mix, and 2 microL FQ-RT Primer Mix. The reaction was incubated at 42  C for 15 min, followed by heat inactivation at 95  C for 3 min. qRT-PCR was carried out using the SGExcel FastSYBR qPCR Mix (Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China) with the following reaction composition: 10 microL 1x MonAmp  SYBR  Green qPCR Mix, 0.4 microL each of 10 microM forward and reverse primers, 2 microL cDNA, and 7.2 microL RNase-Free Water. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 95  C for 30 s; 40 cycles of denaturation at 95  C for 30 s, annealing at 60  C for 40 s, and extension at 72  C for 30 s. Each sample was run in three technical replicates. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2-DeltaDeltaCq method.
Results
Differences in protein content during the grain development process of two oat genotypes

Phenotypic differences between HZ and MC seeds during grain development. A Oat grains from 5 DAF to 30 DAF. White line segments indicate lengths of 1 cm. B Protein content during HZ and MC seed grain development. Error lines indicate standard deviation and "**" indicates significant differences at the P < 0.01 level. C Rate of protein accumsulation during HZ and MC seed grain development

We collected oat seeds at six developmental stages (Fig. 1A) and measured their protein content. Significant differences in protein content were observed between the two varieties across different developmental stages. Both varieties exhibited a gradual increase in protein content, with the high-protein variety HZ showing significantly higher protein levels than MC at all six stages (P < 0.01) (Fig. 1B). The protein accumulation rate followed a "slow-fast-slow" pattern (Fig. 1C). The period from 10 to 15 DAF marked the fastest protein accumulation rate, after which the accumulation rates for both varieties declined continuously (Table S2). Notably, the reduction in the protein accumulation rate from 15 to 20 DAF was less pronounced in HZ compared to MC, which may explain the differences in protein content between the two varieties. Approximately 86% and 88% of the total protein accumulation in HZ and MC, respectively, occurred during these stages. Thus, the period from 10 to 20 DAF was identified as the key phase for oat grain protein accumulation.
Analysis of oat grain metabolites and identification of differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs)

Description of widely targeted metabolomic data of oat seeds at different periods. A Classification ring plots of 1178 metabolites. B Distribution of CV values of the overall sample. C Principal component analysis of metabolites in the overall sample. D Hierarchical clustering heatmap of metabolites in the overall sample. Green to red represents the accumulation level of metabolites from low to high

A total of 1,178 metabolites were identified in this study (Fig. 2A). These metabolites were classified into 13 categories, including 120 alkaloids, 89 amino acids and derivatives, 198 flavonoids, 54 lignans and coumarins, 198 lipids, 44 nucleotides and derivatives, 52 organic acids, 163 phenolic acids, 9 quinones, 70 steroids, 2 tannins, 44 terpenoids, and 44 other metabolites. The total ion chromatogram (TIC) of quality control (QC) samples demonstrated highly overlapping ion current curves, indicating excellent signal stability during repeated mass spectrometry analyses of the same sample (Fig. S1A, B). The Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) extracted ion chromatograms (XIC) revealed overlapping chromatographic peaks among biological replicates, confirming high sample reproducibility (Fig. S1C, D).

The within-group coefficient of variation (CV) was calculated for 21 sample groups, including QC samples, and the distribution of CV values was plotted (Fig. 2B). Approximately 85% of metabolites exhibited CV values below 0.3, indicating stable data and strong within-group reproducibility. Principal component analysis (PCA) of metabolite content data from the 21 samples, including QC samples, showed that Principal Component 1 (PC1) and Principal Component 2 (PC2) accounted for 41.15% and 20.23% of the total variation, respectively. The seven sample groups were clustered into three distinct clusters (Fig. 2C). Cluster 1 included MC10, Cluster 2 included MC20, MC30, HZ10, and quality control (QC) samples, and Cluster 3 included HZ20 and HZ30. This reflects the significant differences in metabolite accumulation during the seed development processes of the two varieties. Moreover, the close clustering of biological replicates of the samples further validates the reliability of sample preparation and data. Hierarchical clustering analysis (Fig. 2D) grouped the three biological replicates from each developmental stage together, confirming the high reliability of the metabolomics data. Metabolites were primarily divided into five groups, representing varying accumulation levels across the three seed development stages.

Orthogonal Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) was applied to analyze the metabolomics data. The R2X, R2Y, and Q2 values were close to 1, indicating a stable and reliable model. Metabolites with VIP values 1 and fold change (FC) 2 (up-regulated) or 0.5 (down-regulated) were identified as differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs).

To elucidate differences in metabolite accumulation between the two oat varieties, pairwise comparisons of metabolites in HZ and MC were conducted at the same developmental stages. In the three comparison groups (HZ10 vs. MC10, HZ20 vs. MC20, and HZ30 vs. MC30), 464 (153 upregulated, 311 downregulated), 359 (158 upregulated, 201 downregulated), and 328 (148 upregulated, 180 downregulated) differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs) were identified, respectively (Fig. S2A-C). Among these, 178 DAMs were common across all three comparison groups, primarily including 6 amino acids and derivatives, 17 lipids, and 97 flavonoids (Fig. 3A, B). Additionally, 191 metabolites exhibited specific differential accumulation only at 10 DAF, including 34 phenolic acids, 32 flavonoids, and 36 lipids (Fig. 3C). At 30 DAF, 17 amino acids and derivatives showed specific differential accumulation (Fig. 3D). The DAMs in the three comparison groups were significantly enriched (P-value < 0.05) in 6, 4, and 37 KEGG pathways, respectively (Fig. 3E). Key pathways included flavonoid biosynthesis (ko00941), biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids (ko01061), linoleic acid metabolism (ko00591), arginine biosynthesis (ko00220), biosynthesis of amino acids (ko01230), and biosynthesis of secondary metabolites (ko01110). Notably, arginine biosynthesis was significantly enriched at both 20 and 30 DAF, while biosynthesis of amino acids and secondary metabolites were enriched at 30 DAF. Linoleic acid metabolism was significantly enriched at both 10 and 20 DAF.

Using 10 DAF as a control, comparisons were made between different developmental stages within each variety. In the four comparison groups for HZ (HZ10 vs. HZ20 and HZ10 vs. HZ30) and MC (MC10 vs. MC20 and MC10 vs. MC30), 384 (108 upregulated, 240 downregulated), 439 (143 upregulated, 296 downregulated), 460 (130 upregulated, 330 downregulated), and 143 (63 upregulated, 80 downregulated) DAMs were identified, respectively (Fig. S3A-D). Among these, 163 DAMs were common across all four comparison groups, primarily including 7 amino acids and derivatives, 33 phenolic acids, 26 flavonoids, 6 organic acids, and 21 lipids (Fig. 4A, B). Specific DAMs unique to the HZ group included 6 amino acids and derivatives, 24 flavonoids, and 15 phenolic acids (Fig. 4C), while the MC group exhibited 12 amino acids and derivatives, 31 flavonoids, and 29 phenolic acids (Fig. 4D). The DAMs in the four comparison groups were significantly enriched (P -value < 0.05) in 3, 0, 5, and 4 KEGG pathways, respectively. Key enriched pathways included valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis (ko00290), pyrimidine metabolism (ko00240), phenylpropanoid biosynthesis (ko00940), pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis (ko00770), linoleic acid metabolism (ko00591), biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids (ko01061), and betaalanine metabolism (ko00410) (Fig. 4E).
Quality control of oat grain transcriptome data and identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs)

To elucidate the molecular mechanisms regulating protein synthesis during oat grain development, RNA-Seq analysis was conducted on grains from both varieties at different developmental stages. The 36 samples yielded 2,372,542,166 raw sequencing reads with an error rate of approximately 0.03%. Quality metrics showed Q30 scores ranging from 93.32% to 94.62% and GC content between 51.36% and 53.24% (Table S3), confirming high sequencing quality suitable for downstream analyses. Pearson correlation analysis of the 36 samples' sequencing data generated a correlation heatmap (Fig. S4A), demonstrating strong correlations (high coefficients) among biological replicates at each developmental stage. This indicated consistent gene expression patterns, meeting the prerequisites for differential gene analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed tight clustering of biological replicates (Fig. S4B), with Principal Components 1 and 2 explaining 31.9% and 14.4% of total variance, respectively. Notably, the two genotypes showed clear separation at each stage, reflecting significant expression differences throughout grain filling. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using thresholds of log2 Fold Change 1 and FDR 0.05 to examine expression variations between genotypes and developmental stages.
Screening and enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in oat grains

Comparative analysis of DEGs between varieties at identical growth stages revealed substantial transcriptional differences. In the six HZ vs. MC comparisons (HZ5 vs. MC5 to HZ30 vs. MC30), we identified 11,432 (5,580 up/5,852 down), 10,106 (4,692 up/5,451 down), 9,750 (4,516 up/5,234 down), 9,278 (4,011.up/5,267 down), 8,637 (3,836 up/4,801 down), and 9,511 (4,171 up/5,340 down) DEGs respectively (Fig. S5A). Notably, 3,777 DEGs were consistently differentially expressed across all six stages (Fig. S5B). Developmental stage comparisons within each variety (using HZ5/MC5 as controls) showed dynamic expression patterns. The ten comparison groups (HZ10-HZ5 to MC30-MC5) exhibited: 1,308 (768 up/540 down), 6,245 (3,318 up/2,927 down), 12,043 (6,082.up/5,961 down), 13,204 (6,726 up/6,478 down), 16,663 (8,410 up/8,253 down), 1,787 (1,357 up/430 down), 9,138 (5,111 up/4,027 down), 11,604 (6,165 up/5,439 down), 15,360 (7,638 up/7,722 down), and 18,424 (8,943 up/9,481 down) DEGs respectively (Fig. S6A, B). Core DEG sets comprised 764 (HZ) and 1,069 (MC) genes shared across all developmental comparisons (Fig. S6C, D).

To analyze the potential functions of these DEGs, we conducted KEGG Pathway enrichment analysis (Fig. S7-9). Among all the comparison groups, the most frequently annotated pathways were Starch and sucrose metabolism (ko00500), Pentose phosphate pathway (ko00030), Glycolysis/Gluconeogenesis (ko00010), Pyruvate metabolism (ko00620), Tyrosine metabolism (ko00350), Tryptophan metabolism (ko00380), Nitrogen metabolism (ko00910), Citrate cycle (ko00020), and Amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism (ko00520).

It is worth noting that the DEGs in the HZ group were more significantly enriched in pathways related to the synthesis and accumulation of proteins and amino acids, such as Amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism (ko00520), Glycolysis/Gluconeogenesis (ko00010), Cyanoamino acid metabolism (ko00460), and Pyruvate metabolism (ko00620). This might be the potential reason why the protein content in HZ was higher than that in MC.

In addition, these DEGs were also significantly enriched in pathways related to the synthesis and metabolism of secondary metabolites and fatty acids, such as Flavonoid biosynthesis (ko00941), Glycerolipid metabolism (ko00561), Fatty acid metabolism (ko01212), Fatty acid elongation (ko00062), Fatty acid degradation (ko00071), and Biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids (ko01040). This might imply that there were potential associations among the metabolic pathways of proteins, flavonoids, and fatty acids.
Screening for genes related to protein and amino acid accumulation via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA)
WGCNA of DEGs in 10, 20, and 30 DAF oat seeds. A Hierarchical clustering plot of DEGs. B Heatmap of correlation between co-expression modules and each trait

To elucidate gene expression dynamics during oat grain development, we performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) on differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Setting the optimal soft threshold at 16, we hierarchically clustered all DEGs into 12 co-expression modules (Fig. 5A). Subsequently, based on the expression matrices of 18 samples at 10, 20, and 30 days after flowering (DAF), we conducted a correlation analysis between gene modules and the quantitative data of proteins and amino acids (including the quantitative data of all 7 amino acids obtained from metabolomics) (Fig. 5B).

The results showed that the correlation coefficient between the blue module and the grain protein content reached 0.92 (p-value < 0.01), and it was extremely significantly (p-value < 0.01) negatively correlated with the contents of DL-Leucine and L-Tyrosine. This module contained 4,151 DEGs. In contrast to the blue module, the turquoise module was extremely significantly (p-value < 0.01) negatively correlated with the protein content and was extremely signifi- cantly (p-value < 0.01) or significantly (p-value < 0.05) positively correlated with the contents of DL-Leucine and L-Tyrosine. This indicated that the gene functions in the blue and turquoise modules might be opposite. The red module was positively correlated (p-value < 0.01) with L-Arginine, L-Histidine, L-Ornithine, and L-Tryptophan, with correlation coefficients of 0.85, 0.82, 0.83, and 0.74 respectively, and was negatively correlated with the protein content, although it did not reach a significant level. This module contained 662 DEGs. In addition, the purple module had the same correlations with various traits as the red module, and we considered that the genes in these two modules might have similar functions. Furthermore, the brown module was extremely significantly (p-value.< 0.01) negatively correlated with the protein content, and the expression of these genes might lead to protein degradation or hinder protein synthesis. The connectivity value (k-value) of the DEGs in each module was calculated, and the gene with the largest k-value in each module was identified as the hub gene of that module. The IDs and annotations of these hub genes are shown in Table 1. These hub genes might play a crucial role in the synthesis and accumulation of proteins and amino acids in oat grains. KEGG enrichment of key modules (Fig. S10) revealed: The results showed that the DEGs in the blue module were mainly enriched in pathways such as the Citrate cycle (ko00020), Pyruvate metabolism (ko00620), and Alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism (ko00250). The DEGs in the brown module were mainly enriched in pathways such as Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (ko04141) and Ubiquitin mediated proteolysis (ko04120). The DEGs in the red module were mainly enriched in pathways such as MAPK signaling pathway - plant (ko04016), Ubiquitin mediated proteolysis (ko04120), and Tryptophan metabolism (ko00380). The DEGs in the purple module were mainly enriched in pathways such as Biosynthesis of secondary metabolites (ko01110), Carotenoid biosynthesis (ko00906), and Alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism (ko00250). The DEGs in the turquoise module were significantly (p-value < 0.05) enriched in a total of 52 pathways, and the top 20 most significant pathways included Biosynthesis of amino acids (ko01230), Glycolysis/Gluconeogenesis (ko00010), Valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation (ko00280), Pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis (ko00770), Biotin metabolism (ko00780), Fatty acid metabolism (ko01212), and Fatty acid biosynthesis (ko00061).
