passages.text: Medical images contain information indiscernible to the naked eye,, which can be extracted using radiomic features, a set of statistical and spatial interrelationships between selected voxels in an image. Machine learning (ML) models can harness these radiomic features to predict clinical outcomes,. Radiomics-based ML could potentially detect lung cancer earlier than the current standard of care. However, there are two major barriers to creating radiomics-based early detection models in a clinical context. First, radiomic features are sensitive to image acquisition protocols which vary across and within clinics. These non-biological sources of variation make it difficult to meaningfully combine data or reproduce results. Second, there is a low occurrence rate of cancer in PNs which are very small or early in their development:the target PNs in the early detection problem. For example, when Lung-RADS classifications were applied to scans from the National Lung Screening Trial in a retrospective study, only 0.39% of patients with PNs classified as benign or probably benign at baseline would be diagnosed with cancer after follow-up.

To address this class imbalance and potentially improve model performance, ML training data may be augmented with radiomic features from confirmed benign and malignant PNs later in their development. However, including these PNs in a training set may exacerbate the challenge of radiomic features' dependence on acquisition protocols, especially when biological differences in later-development benign and malignant PNs cause their scans to be affected differently by acquisition protocols. For example, contrast enhancement (CE), administered during scans for cases with clinical concern, tends to accumulate more in tumors than in healthy tissue. Both the frequency and the effect of CE create a quasi-systematic difference between later-development benign and malignant PNs that their radiomic features might inherit when calculated from routine imaging.

To mitigate effects of variable image acquisition parameters and improve generalizability of models, ComBat ("Combine Batches") harmonization can learn corrective transformations to remove acquisition-related bias, from radiomic feature distributions,,. In CT-based radiomics for lung cancer, ComBat has been applied mostly in predictive pipelines addressing outcomes like recurrence, development-free survival, and overall survival. These predictive problems use data from only malignant PNs. In contrast, lung cancer diagnosis models require data from both benign and malignant PNs. Some studies have implemented ComBat when combining radiomic data from benign and malignant tissues, but most of these have corrected for multi-center overall effects rather than variation in specific acquisition protocols,,. The challenge of harmonizing radiomic features from benign and malignant tissues resembles the challenge of harmonizing features from tissues of different origin. Previous studies have considered methods of applying ComBat to harmonize radiomic feature data from tissues of different origin (breast tumor and healthy liver tissue) when acquisition protocols vary, including harmonizing with tissue type as a covariate and harmonizing different tissue types separately,. The best practice for harmonizing benign and malignant forms of the same tissue:such as lung tumor and benign lung tissue:for specific acquisition protocols has not yet been established.

To develop radiomics-based models that can accurately predict the malignancy of PNs at their earliest development from routine clinical imaging, we augmented training with later-development benign and malignant PNs and accounted for non-standardized acquisition using ComBat harmonization. To remove radiomic features' dependence on four acquisition parameters, we compared three methods of harmonizing augmented training sets: 1) harmonizing all training data collectively in the standard manner, with no biological distinction, 2) harmonizing with a covariate to distinguish early-development data, later-development benign augmentation data, and later-development malignant augmentation data, and 3) harmonizing these three datasets separately. We compared the performance of lung cancer early detection models trained on augmented data harmonized using these methods.
Results
Baseline radiomic model for early detection

To evaluate radiomics-based early detection of lung cancer, we collected a dataset containing clinical chest CT scans of early-development PNs. Because physicians primarily interpret scans based on PN size and rate of growth, we use physicians' interpretation at the time of a given scan as an indicator of PN development. For the purposes of this study, all PNs interpreted at time of scan as benign, probably benign, or indeterminate are considered early-development. Each PN was scanned multiple times separated by interims of months, and each scan had a corresponding time-of-scan interpretation.

The PNs imaged in the early-development scans received follow-up. At the end of follow-up, some PNs were diagnosed as benign and some PNs were diagnosed as malignant (details in Methods). We refer to this as a PN's endpoint diagnosis, which may differ from its time-of-scan diagnoses (for examples, see Supplementary Fig. S1). The early-development scans of PNs with an endpoint malignant diagnosis show the earliest onset of lung cancer. Overall, the early-development dataset had only 16.6% incidence of cancer (Table 1). Throughout this study, we evaluate model performance using held-out test data drawn only from this early-development dataset.

We developed a predictive pipeline using this data, shown schematically in Fig. 1. PNs were segmented in the CT images using semi-automated contouring software. Scans were preprocessed (see Methods) and a total of 107 radiomic features were extracted for each scan of a PN using the open-source Python library PyRadiomics (Fig. 1a). This early-development dataset was randomly split into five folds while ensuring no patients overlap between training and test sets, repeated 10 times (50 trials; Fig. 1b).

The dataset included scans acquired using non-standardized parameters, including kilovoltage peak (KVP), focal spots, scanner manufacturer, and CE. For each training set, we used Optimized Permutation Nested ComBat (OPNCB), which applies ComBat to remove biases from multiple protocols sequentially, to correct for variability in these four parameters (Fig. 1c). Scans with rare acquisition protocols were excluded from a trial when ComBat could not learn a correction due to insufficient samples of that protocol.

To predict PN endpoint diagnosis from harmonized radiomic features, we trained a two-stage predictive model. First, a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selected a subset of predictive features (Fig. 1d). From all radiomic features, LASSO selected an average of 3.8 [3.3-4.4] (n = 49; brackets indicate the 95% confidence interval here and henceforth) features per trial. Next, a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) used selected features from the training set to classify PNs by endpoint diagnosis, benign or malignant (Fig. 1e).

The trained ComBat estimators, feature selection results, and trained SVM were applied to the held-out test set for each trial (Fig. 1F). The ComBat algorithm failed for one trial's test set due to insufficient sample sizes within the test set, so this trial was excluded from all further consideration in this study. This model trained on only early-development data achieved an average ROC-AUC of 0.58 [0.51-0.64] (n = 49) for the test set. This performance is near chance, motivating our hypothesis that augmenting the training set with additional data may improve early detection model performance.
Training set augmentation with radiomic features from later-development PNs

To improve performance, we added radiomic feature data from benign and malignant PNs later in their development (n = 225 scans, see Table 1) to the early-development training data. For the purposes of this study, PNs interpreted at time of scan as suspicious or malignant are later-development. We refer to later-development benign and malignant scans as augmentation datasets because they augment early-development training data but are not used to test performance. We will refer to training sets that contain data from both the early-development dataset and the augmentation datasets as augmented training sets. Figure 2 visualizes our scan classification scheme, where the early-development dataset is shown in purple. Supplementary Figure S1 follows three representative PNs to further clarify our classification scheme. The malignant dataset holds later-development scans of PNs that were later confirmed as malignant using PET/CT or biopsy (red in Fig. 2). The benign dataset holds later-development scans of PNs that were later confirmed as benign using wedge resection or biopsy (blue in Fig. 2). Both augmentation datasets include follow-up scans of PNs that have previous scans in the early-development dataset. If a patient appeared in a trial's test set, no later-development scans from that patient were included in that trial's training set. When augmentation datasets were included, occurrence of cancer increased from 16.6-53.4% in our total data pool (Table 1), removing the previous class imbalance. We added these augmentation datasets to the original early-development training sets in all trials and trained early detection models following the pipeline in Fig. 3.

Both augmentation datasets were also highly variable in our acquisition parameters of interest (Supplementary Table S1). To evaluate acquisition dependence of radiomic features in each augmented training set, we developed a procedure using the Kruskal-Wallis test, see Methods. A significant result (p <= 0.05) indicated that a given feature was acquisition-dependent. Table 2 summarizes feature dependence of acquisition parameters and Fig. 4 shows p-values for acquisition dependence of each feature and acquisition parameter from a sample trial. Without harmonization, 12.1% [11.2-13.1%] of radiomic features were acquisition-independent (n = 49 trials, Fig. 4 top row). To mitigate effects of acquisition variation within each trial, we applied OPNCB to learn corrective transformations from the entire augmented training set (hereafter: collective harmonization, Fig. 3 bottom left), and features which remained acquisition dependent were excluded from further analysis in each trial (Fig. 3c*). However, collective harmonization lowered the proportion of acquisition-independent features to 2.6% [2.2-3.1%] (n = 49 trials; Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 1.6e-08). Collective harmonization increased CE dependence, and consequently total acquisition dependence, compared to unharmonized data for both benign and malignant augmentation datasets (Table 2 and Fig. 4 second row).
Comparing harmonization methods to remove acquisition dependence in augmented training sets

Collective harmonization assumed each acquisition protocol biased a radiomic feature in the same way across all three datasets, yet this assumption may be invalid due to biological and acquisitional differences between early-development, later-development benign, and later-development malignant datasets. Radiomic features in later-development benign and malignant datasets may have different distributions due to their biological differences independent of acquisition. Specific protocols are used to acquire scans in different datasets at different frequencies (Supplementary Table S1), further influencing the feature distributions. Using ComBat with a covariate:an added corrective parameter learned for a specific dataset:accounts for this difference in distributions, while still assuming a protocol has the same effect on scans in different datasets. A transformation applied to scans in different datasets has the same slope but a net shift in intercept.

When a protocol has different effects on scans in different datasets, corresponding corrective transformations may have to differ between datasets in both intercept and slope. Because ComBat estimates acquisition effects from all input data, datasets with different acquisition effects (additive or multiplicative) should be harmonized separately. For example, different tissue types (breast tumor and healthy liver tissue) require distinct ComBat transformations to correct for acquisition variability due to their biological differences.

CE exemplifies a difference in both the means and acquisition effects between our later-development benign and malignant augmentation datasets. Later-development scans administered with CE due to clinical concern are more likely to be malignant than benign (Supplementary Table S1), creating a difference in mean for some radiomic features, and contrast medium is expected to accumulate more in tumors than in healthy tissues, creating a difference in acquisition effect for some radiomic features. Collectively harmonized features exhibited frequent acquisition dependence due to CE, indicating that collective harmonization does not handle these differences well.

Thus, to account for baseline and acquisition differences between biologically distinct PNs, we compared the additional methods of applying the OPNCB algorithm: 1) harmonizing with a covariate to distinguish early-development, late-development benign, and late-development malignant datasets (hereafter: covariate harmonization, Fig. 3 bottom center), or 2) harmonizing early-development, late-development benign, and late-development malignant datasets separately (hereafter: separate harmonization, Fig. 3 bottom right).

When all augmentation data was added to the training set (Fig. 3c*), the proportion of acquisition-independent features defined by Kruskal-Wallis averaged 12.3% [11.4-13.3%] (n = 49 trials) with covariate harmonization, and 86.9% [84.4-89.5%] (n = 49 trials) with separate harmonization. The frequency of each radiomic feature's net acquisition dependence after each method:how often the distribution of that feature was dependent on at least one acquisition parameter:is given in Supplementary Table S2. When comparing metrics for the three methods, adjusted p-values were calculated using Holm-Bonferroni. Covariate harmonization significantly increased the proportion of acquisition-independent features compared to collective harmonization (Wilcoxon signed-rank, adjusted p = 1.4e-09, n = 49). Separate harmonization significantly increased the proportion of acquisition-independent features compared to both collective harmonization (Wilcoxon signed-rank, adjusted p = 1.4e-09, n = 49) and covariate harmonization (Wilcoxon signed-rank, adjusted p = 1.9e-115, n = 49).
Impact of training set augmentation and harmonization method on early detection models

To observe how the performance of early detection models scales with the amount of added training data, we constructed a learning curve by varying the fraction of the augmentation datasets added to each training set. For each level of augmentation of each training set, LASSO-SVM models were trained on features harmonized using collective, covariate, or separate harmonization, creating three versions of a model for each augmented training set. We refer to these models as collective, covariate, and separate harmonization models depending on the harmonization method applied during training.

While covariate and separate harmonization distinguish benign and malignant PNs in the augmentation datasets, they make no such distinction when harmonizing the early-development dataset. Applying the trained ComBat estimators to the test set, which is drawn only from the early-development dataset, uses no foreknowledge of whether each PN is benign or malignant. Thus, test set performance simulates clinical application for early detection where the endpoint diagnosis is unknown.

When increasing the amount of augmentation data included in training, we found that collective harmonization models' performance failed to improve (Fig. 5a left). In contrast, accounting for biological differences when harmonizing augmentation data enabled LASSO-SVM models to improve as more training data was added. We observed logarithmic scaling between augmentation fraction and test ROC-AUC for both covariate ( R2 = 0.95, Fig. 5a center) and separate ( R2 = 0.94, Fig. 5a right) harmonization models.

When 100% of augmentation data were added to the training set, models achieved average test ROC-AUC of 0.50 [0.44-0.56] (n = 45) for collective harmonization, 0.72 [0.67-0.76] (n = 49) for covariate harmonization, and 0.69 [0.63-0.74] (n = 49) for separate harmonization (Fig. 5B). All but one of collective harmonization models could not separate benign and malignant classes and classified all samples as benign. According to the Delong test, the difference between test ROC-AUC of separate and collective harmonization models was significant (adjusted p <= 0.05) for 24.4% of trials (n = 45), where separate harmonization outperformed collective harmonization. The difference between covariate and collective harmonization models was also significant for 28.8% of trials (n = 45), where covariate harmonization outperformed collective harmonization. The difference between separate and covariate harmonization models was significant for 6.1% of trials (n = 49), where covariate harmonization outperformed separate harmonization. The weighted accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of predictions on test samples are reported in Table 3. Covariate harmonization models outperformed separate harmonization in sensitivity (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.014, n = 49) but covariate and separate harmonization models did not show a significant difference in specificity.
Predictive features in early detection models with augmented training sets

We again focus our analysis on trials where 100% of augmentation data were added to the training set. From features which were acquisition-independent post-harmonization, LASSO selected an average of 1.0 [0.8-1.3] (n = 45) features per trial for collective harmonization, 3.5 [3.0-4.1] (n = 49) for covariate harmonization, and 7.4 [6.7-8.3] (n = 49) for separate harmonization. The most frequently selected features varied by harmonization method: Flatness for collective harmonization, GLCM informational measure of correlation 1 for covariate harmonization, and Flatness, Sphericity, NGTDM Strength, and GLDM Small Dependence High Gray Level Emphasis for separate harmonization. Some of these features have been related to lung cancer,. Complete feature selection frequencies are detailed in Supplementary Table S3.
Discussion

The value of a radiomics-based machine learning model for lung cancer early detection is determined by its applicability to clinical scenarios, which must overcome both an inherent sample class imbalance and non-standardized image acquisition. In this study, we addressed class imbalance by augmenting training data with later-development benign and malignant PNs and addressed acquisition variability using ComBat harmonization. Correcting acquisition effects is essential for clinical utility because models trained on acquisition-dependent radiomic features do not generalize well to new sites, or rare acquisition protocols. Models trained without harmonization:using acquisition-dependent data:may appear to exhibit good performance. Using our datasets, LASSO-SVMs with unharmonized augmented training sets achieved an average ROC-AUC of 0.76 [0.71,0.81] (n = 49) on unharmonized test sets. But this outcome is likely an artifact of site-specific acquisition effects that differ distinctively between benign and malignant PNs. These effects prevent such a model from being generalizable and are precisely what harmonization aims to remove.

Harmonization becomes complicated when augmenting training data with later-development PNs because radiomic features from biologically distinct PNs:early-development PNs, later-development benign PNs, later-development malignant PNs:may each need distinct corrections to compensate for acquisition variability. Returning to our previous example, CE may have a large effect on feature distributions from later-development malignant PNs, which have enhanced permeability and retention, while having a smaller effect on features from later-development benign PNs (e.g. see graph for unharmonized data in Fig. 4). While we focus our analysis on differences across later-development datasets, features of early-development PNs may also show distributions distinct from those of later-development PNs, one example being PN volume.

Incorrectly harmonized radiomic features may mislead a model rather than improve performance. Indeed, when harmonization did not distinguish biologically distinct later-development PNs, we found that performance decreased with larger amounts of augmentation data. Thus, we evaluated methods of distinguishing biologically distinct PNs during harmonization. While collective harmonization applied identical corrections to all datasets, separate and covariate harmonization learned corrections specific to each biologically distinct dataset (Fig. 3). Covariate harmonization accounted for dataset-specific feature distributions and separate harmonization further accounted for dataset-specific acquisition effects. Both separate and covariate harmonization recovered acquisition-independent distributions in benign and malignant augmentation training data for significantly more features than collective harmonization, indicating that radiomic features of later-development benign and malignant PNs need distinct corrections. Separate harmonization removed acquisition dependence from significantly more features than covariate harmonization, indicating that acquisition protocols have different effects on benign and malignant PNs for many radiomic features (Supplementary Table S2).

Accordingly harmonized radiomic features from benign and malignant PNs could effectively augment the training of lung cancer early detection models. However, because separate harmonization partitions the data into smaller subsets before learning corrections, its corrections are limited by a smaller sample size than covariate harmonization. If we increase sample size by relaxing our scan inclusion criteria and adding benign PNs that did not receive follow-up (n = 156) to the early-development dataset, the performance of 100% augmented separate harmonization models (ROC-AUC 0.72 [0.69-0.76]) matches that of 100% augmented covariate harmonization models (ROC-AUC 0.73 [0.68-0.77]). Overcoming these sample size limitations and confirming our results on a larger dataset is a promising direction of future study.

The impacts of our acquisition parameters of interest have been studied,,,. Our datasets are heterogeneous in several additional acquisition parameters (e.g. scanner model and convolution kernel) which could not be controlled for in this study due to high variation and consequently small sample size for specific protocols. Further, lung cancer type (e.g. squamous cell, adenocarcinoma) for malignant scans was not uniform and these biological differences may also impact acquisition effects within malignant PNs.

This study aimed to closely simulate a clinical application scenario for radiomics-based lung cancer early detection. Our datasets were gathered from a clinical setting and had high acquisition variability, providing a realistic test of harmonization methods for a clinical early detection scenario. While covariate and separate harmonization account for biological differences in augmentation training data, the endpoint diagnosis is unknown when harmonizing and classifying scans in the early-development dataset, as in the clinic. Scans in our early-development dataset are those actually seen in clinical early detection efforts. As such, some uncertainty in the endpoint diagnosis of these scans, and thus the target classification for the ML model, is inherited from the clinical process. This uncertainty is obvious for PNs when their benign endpoint diagnosis is unconfirmed. To mitigate this uncertainty, we include unconfirmed benign PNs only when at least two scans were performed to demonstrate stability over time, but this remains a limitation of our study. Nonetheless, such PNs constitute most of what is seen in lung cancer screening and including these in our dataset faithfully simulates the clinical scenario. Early-development scans with a malignant endpoint diagnosis also have an uncertain ML classification because the PN may not have developed malignant characteristics by the time of scan. On the other hand, these scans are central to modeling lung cancer detection at its earliest onset.

To meaningfully combine radiomic feature data from early-development and later-development PNs and harness this information for early lung cancer detection, we must first establish methods to remove acquisition dependence from these different data types. Based on our analysis, we recommend harmonizing radiomic features from early-development, later-development benign, and later-development malignant PNs either separately or with a covariate. Our finding that acquisition effects differ between benign and malignant tissues of the same tissue origin may extend to other cancer types and investigating this is a direction of future study. Studying these harmonization methods is an important step towards radiomics as a clinically viable quantitative tool for detecting lung cancer at its earliest onset, which could allow malignant tumors to be treated months earlier and reduce unnecessary resection and imaging procedures, reducing healthcare costs and improving patient outcomes.
Methods
Radiomic dataset acquisition

This retrospective study was approved by the UVA Institutional Review Board (IRB) (approval number: 301447), and due to its retrospective nature, informed consent was waived by the UVA IRB. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. We acquired chest CT scans of PNs from the University of Virginia hospital. Physician annotations and comments on scans were available for all PNs. If resection, biopsy, or PET/CT were performed, these results were available. Some patients had multiple PNs and some PNs had multiple follow-up scans separated by interims of months (Table 1).

All PNs in the early-development dataset were interpreted as benign, probably benign, or indeterminate at time of scan. Keyword indicators of this physician interpretation were, in order of the priority with which they were used to classify scans: benign (Lung-RADS category 2), probably benign (Lung-RADS category 3), inflammatory/infectious, indeterminate, 12-month follow-up (without verbal indication of suspicion), 6-month follow-up (without verbal indication of suspicion).

After follow-up, PNs from scans in the early-development dataset either received a malignant diagnosis, confirmed by biopsy or PET/CT, a benign diagnosis, confirmed by biopsy or wedge resection, or showed no indicators of becoming malignant. These last PNs are presumed benign, supported by at least one follow-up scan but without an additional diagnosis method.

All scans in our augmentation datasets were interpreted as suspicious or malignant at time of scan. Keyword indicators of this physician interpretation were, in order of priority: malignant, known cancer, very suspicious (Lung-RADS category 4B), suspicious (Lung-RADS category 4A), possibility for neoplasm, recommendation for PET/CT or biopsy (without verbal indication of indeterminate or alternative diagnosis).

The malignant augmentation dataset holds scans of PNs that were later confirmed as malignant by biopsy or PET/CT. The benign augmentation dataset holds scans of PNs that were later confirmed as benign by biopsy or wedge resection.

CT images for all datasets were acquired in DICOM format. CE information was noted from scan protocol comments and all other acquisition parameter information was extracted from the DICOM header files. To acquire segmentations, images were displayed with the lung viewing setting. Following physician annotations, each region of interest corresponding to a PN in the CT images was segmented using semi-automated contouring tools in Varian's Velocity AI software by one of three raters.

Pixel data and segmentations were extracted from the DICOM files. Because radiomic texture features require voxels to be rotationally invariant the PyRadiomics feature extractor was used to resample images and masks to cubic-mm voxels. Lanczos interpolation was used for the images for greatest reproducibility and nearest-neighbor interpolation was used for segmentation masks. To ensure all air and bone voxels were excluded and to improve reproducibility, voxels with intensities outside - 700 to 500 Hounsfield Units were excluded from calculations of non-shape features. Other radiomic studies of PNs have used narrower thresholds to analyze only malignant tissue but we chose a less conservative threshold because we also analyzed benign tissue and very small PNs. All other PyRadiomics feature extractor settings were left at default values. A total of 107 features were extracted from all regions of interest.
Formation of training and test sets for cross-validation of early detection models

In our baseline early detection pipeline, the early-development dataset was split into five folds using a randomized Group Stratified K-fold (scikit-learn) to ensure no patients overlap between training and test sets, repeated 10 times for a total of 50 unique training and test sets.

In our early detection pipeline with training set augmentation, we began with the same splits of the early-development dataset as used to validate the baseline model (50 unique training and test sets), and augmentation data were added to these training sets. For a given trial, scans were not used to augment the training set if the same patient appeared in that trial's test set; such augmentation scans were unavailable to that trial. For each early-development train-test split, we varied the fraction of available augmentation data included in the corresponding training set: 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% (8 unique fractions). Training set augmentation was cumulative. This gave a total of 50x8 = 400 unique augmented training sets corresponding to the 50 test sets.
Harmonization of training and test sets

This study used OPNCB to correct for acquisition parameters. In OPNCB, harmonization is performed for each acquisition parameter iteratively in an order which removes acquisition dependency from the most features, as compared to other permutations. Because ComBat is a data-driven method, no phantom imaging is required for this standardization.

We studied three methods of applying OPNCB to a given training set. In collective harmonization, OPNCB was applied to the complete training set, where extracted radiomic features and corresponding scan acquisition information were the inputs. In separate harmonization, the training set was separated by dataset before applying OPNCB to these subsets individually. In covariate harmonization, OPNCB was applied to the complete training set, and a dataset label for each scan was supplied as an additional input.

OPNCB was performed on training sets and the trained ComBat estimators were applied to the corresponding test sets using the function neuroComBatFromTraining being developed by Fortin et al.,. The estimators appropriate to the acquisition parameters of a given test sample were applied in the order determined for the training set by the OPNCB algorithm. For separate harmonization, estimators applied to the test set were those learned for the early-development training scans alone.

ComBat fails if fewer than three training samples were acquired with the same protocol, e.g., if only two scans were acquired using a certain focal spot size. In such cases, these scans were excluded from the trial. If a protocol was used to acquire a scan in a test set but was not used to acquire any scan in the training set, that scan was also excluded from the trial, because no estimator was trained for that protocol. We developed an automated process to perform scan exclusion based on these criteria.

In our baseline early detection pipeline, OPNCB was applied using collective harmonization. In our early detection pipeline with training set augmentation, for each of our augmented training sets, we applied OPNCB using our three examined methods in parallel, leading to 3 versions of a given augmented training set and corresponding test set.
Evaluation of acquisition dependence of radiomic features

In our early detection pipeline with training set augmentation, to evaluate whether harmonization removed acquisition dependence from augmented training sets, we used the Kruskal-Wallis test to compare feature distributions grouped by instances of acquisition parameters. For example, feature distributions from CE scans were compared to those from non-CE scans. The test was run separately on the benign and malignant augmentation training data, because correct feature distributions should be consistent across acquisition within benign PNs or within malignant PNs, though benign and malignant distributions may differ. The test was not performed on the early-development training data because of this additional source of variability. For a given radiomic feature, if the test was significant (p <= 0.05) for either benign or malignant samples, that feature was deemed acquisition dependent. This procedure was applied to all 107 features.

To validate this procedure, we applied it to randomized splits of unharmonized scans that were acquired with the same protocols of interest:i.e. "acquisition-independent." Our datasets contained 11 such uniform groups, ranging in size from 8 to 114 scans. These uniform groups contained both benign and malignant samples. The procedure defined an average 98.2% [97.8-98.5%] (n = 55) of features to be acquisition-independent as expected. This supports Kruskal-Wallis as a reasonable test to define acquisition dependence. Variability in unaccounted-for acquisition parameters most likely caused nonzero deviation from normal distributions.
Feature selection and classifier training

To increase the generalization of a predictive model and thus better model clinical applicability, we used a LASSO to select predictive features (regularization parameter alpha = 0.05) from each training set. Radiomic features were standardized to have zero mean and unit variance using the StandardScaler function from the Python library scikit-learn before LASSO was applied to select features. In our baseline pipeline, LASSO was applied to all radiomic features. In our pipeline with training set augmentation, LASSO was applied only to radiomic features which were acquisition-independent according to the Kruskal-Wallis test.

LASSO-selected standardized features from the training set were used to train a binary SVM (regularization parameter C = 1) whose target was PN malignancy (class 0: endpoint benign diagnosis, class 1: endpoint malignant diagnosis). A linear kernel was chosen for the SVM to avoid overfitting. If harmonization failed or no features were selected in a given trial, an SVM was not trained for that trial.
Feature selection results and the trained SVM were applied to the held-out harmonized test set corresponding to each training set.
Statistical analyses

We used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to compare performance metrics between methods in trials where all models were trained. The Kruskal-Wallis test was adopted to compare feature distributions. Confidence intervals for continuous variables were calculated using the t-distribution and confidence intervals for discrete variables (e.g. numbers of selected features) were calculated using the Poisson distribution. These statistical tests were all conducted in Python using the SciPy library. The predictive performance of ML models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating curve (ROC-AUC), weighted accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, all of which were calculated using the Python library scikit-learn. The Delong test was used to compare ROC-AUC curves and was conducted in Python using the MLstatkit library.

All p-values reported in this study are two-tailed. Adjusted p-values were calculated with Holm-Bonferroni using the multipletests function from the Python statsmodels library to control for multiple comparisons across the three harmonization methods.

passages.text: Integrating transcriptome and metabolome reveals sex-dependent meat quality regulation in Qiandongnan Xiaoxiang chickens

This study integrated metabolomics and transcriptomics to elucidate molecular mechanisms regulating meat quality in Qiandongnan Xiaoxiang chickens across sexes and muscle types. Male chickens exhibited significantly higher shear force in breast and leg muscles (P < 0.01) and lower cooking loss in leg muscle (P < 0.05) compared to females. Metabolomic profiling identified 24 sex-differential metabolites, enriched in amino acid and nicotinate metabolism pathways. Transcriptomic analysis revealed 377 and 486 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in breast and leg muscles between sexes, respectively, associated with steroid biosynthesis and energy metabolism. Integrative analysis highlighted histidine metabolism (characterized by anserine accumulation in females via MAOA upregulation) and nicotinate metabolism as key sex-specific pathways. Tissue comparisons demonstrated distinct regulation of linoleic acid metabolism, purine metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. These findings provide novel insights into molecular networks underlying meat quality differences and identify potential biomarkers for enhancing nutritional value in poultry breeding.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12864-025-12316-z.
Introduction

Broiler chickens are highly favored due to their superior quality, affordability, and short production cycle. Importantly, they provide consumers with a safe and reliable source of animal protein. Recently, extensive research has focused on enhancing meat quality, as consumers increasingly prioritize the nutritional value and health benefits of their food. The breast muscle of broilers, in particular, has garnered attention due to its direct correlation with both muscle yield and meat quality characteristics. Meat quality is a multifaceted trait influenced by various physicochemical characteristics, including pH, tenderness, meat color, intramuscular fat content, fatty acid composition, and sensory quality. However, sex also plays a crucial role in determining these physicochemical parameters, as well as the growth and slaughter performance of broilers.

The evident impact of sexual dimorphism on the size of carcasses directly affects other parameters of the slaughter performance of chickens and the quality of meat. Researchers have investigated the chemical composition of the breast muscles of male and female farmed pheasants. Research has revealed that sex affects the total collagen content, suggesting that the tenderness and shear force of meat may vary between sexes. Dariusz et al. (2018) reported that the shear force values of the breast muscle in 112-day-old male pheasants were greater than those in female pheasants. Furthermore, since sexual dimorphism is believed to influence meat quality, one explanation for the variations in meat quality could be the differences in androgen levels between sexes. These hormones significantly impact lipid metabolism in birds. Smiecinska et al. (2024) demonstrated that muscle type (leg vs. breast) significantly influences both individual fatty acid (FA) content and the overall FA profile of intramuscular fat (IMF) in poultry. Furthermore, research indicates that hen muscle tissue contains higher inosine monophosphate (IMP) concentrations than rooster muscle tissue, with breast muscle exhibiting significantly greater IMP levels than leg muscle. Compared to breast muscle, leg muscle displays higher pH, increased cooking loss, reduced lightness (L*), and lower drip loss.

Metabolomics quantitatively and qualitatively analyzes small-molecule metabolites. LC-MS technology enhances chromatographic separation and enables precise metabolite mass measurement with improved sensitivity, accuracy, and precision. RNA-Seq extensively characterizes genetic expression differences related to meat quality. Li et al. (2022) used LC-MS/MS metabolomics to study chicken meat composition across growth stages, revealing significant variations in metabolites like pentadecanoic acid and identifying key functional genes influencing chemical composition and metabolic pathways, such as DGAT2, CYP2D6, APOV1, PLTP and PNMT. This provided insights into metabolic changes during growth and highlighted regulatory genes affecting meat quality and flavor. The integrative analysis of the metabolome and transcriptome would be a breakthrough in identifying the function of unknown genes and determining the gene-to-metabolite correlations. These data could enhance our understanding of chicken physiology, aiding in better breeding and production practices.

The Qiandongnan Xiaoxiang chicken is a distinctive indigenous breed known for its exceptional meat quality and rich flavor. Primarily raised in the southeast region of Guizhou Province, China, this breed is characterized by unique features, such as vibrant feathers and black bones. They are typically raised for 5-6 months before market sale to achieve optimal taste and texture. Few studies to date have examined the effects of sex using integrated transcriptome and metabolome analyses. Furthermore, molecular characterization of their meat quality is limited. In this study, we conducted joint transcriptome and metabolome analyses to investigate metabolite level changes between female and male Qiandongnan Xiaoxiang chickens. Additionally, we examined key pathways differentially regulated between breast and leg muscles. These findings may elucidate underlying mechanisms and identify potential biomarkers for selection strategies to enhance chicken meat nutritional value.
Materials and methods
Animals and sample collection

The animals used in this experiment were provided by the Guizhou Rongjiang Shanong Development Co., Ltd. One-day-old male and female chickens were randomly selected and subjected to identical conditions, including free access to both water and a regulated diet, until they reached 20 weeks of age. A three-phase feeding regimen was implemented following the protocol outlined in Daszkiewicz et al. (2020). The basal diet was formulated to meet the nutrient requirements of Nutrient Requirements of Chinese MeatType Yellow Feathered Chickens. Detailed information on the chemical composition of the diets administered to the chickens can be found in Table S1. Chicks were randomly distributed into pens in a conventional indoor facility. The facility contained fans to ventilate and cool the pens. Each indoor pen was the size of 1.8 mx1.8 m and contained wood shavings, water bowls, and hanging tube feeders. The chicken bred indoor pens were supplied with a constant photoperiod of 24 h. Male (roosters, n = 30) and female (hens, n = 30) Qiandongnan Xiaoxiang chickens were slaughtered at 20 weeks of age. Prior to being slaughtered, the chickens underwent a 12-hour fasting period, although they were given free access to water. They were humanely stunned via a stun bath and subsequently euthanized by cutting. The leg muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, and extensor digitorum longus) and breast muscles were collected for analysis. The samples were placed in sterile tubes and fast-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and then they were transferred to a -80  C ultra-low temperature refrigerator for subsequent metabolome analysis. Muscle tissue from the same chicken was collected in a sterile tube, and quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen, then stored at -80  C for subsequent transcriptome and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis. Samples were designated as: F*_T (female leg muscle, Group A), F*_X (female breast muscle, Group B), M*_T (male leg muscle, Group C), and M*_X (male breast muscle, Group D).
Meat quality measurement

Thirty individual chickens, comprising both males and females, were randomly selected for measurement of meat quality characteristics. The pH of the breast meat was measured twice: once at 45 min postslaughter and again at 24 h postslaughter. This measurement was performed via a precise two-point calibration method, employing standard pH buffers of 4.0 and 7.0, in accordance with established protocols. Drip loss was measured as a percentage of the initial weight of the meat samples compared to their weight after being stored for 24 h at 4  C. Cooking loss was calculated by the weight difference between the fresh samples and the heat-treated samples. Meat color parameters, including lightness (L*), redness (a*) and yellowness (b*), were measured at 24 h postmortem at 4  C with a CR-400 chromometer (Konica Minolta Inc., Tokyo, Japan). Tenderness was assessed via a digital tenderness meter (C-LM4, Tenovo, Beijing, China) operating at a speed of 200 mm/min.

passages.text: Metabolite extraction and data analysis

For each experimental group (F*_T, F*_X, M*_T, M*_X), tissue samples from three independent biological replicates were analyzed. Following dissection, pectoral and leg muscle tissues were immediately flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen tissues were then sectioned into approximately 80 mg fragments on dry ice. These fragments were transferred to 2 mL Eppendorf tubes and homogenized with 200 microL of ultrapure water using five ceramic beads in a mechanical homogenizer. For metabolite extraction, precisely weighed tissue samples were placed in 2 mL centrifuge tubes containing 1000 microL of extraction solution (75% methanol: chloroform [9:1] and 25% water) along with three stainless steel beads. Homogenization was performed using a bead mill, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4  C. The resulting supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 mum membrane into LC-MS vials for subsequent analysis.

LC analysis was conducted via an ACQUITY UPLC System (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). Chromatographic separation was achieved with an ACQUITY UPLC  HSS T3 column (150 x 2.1 mm, 1.8 mum) (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). The column temperature was maintained at 40  C. The mobile phase consisted of water with 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). The flow rate was set to 0.3 mL/min, and the gradient elution was programmed as follows: 0-1 min, 95% A; 1-10 min, 95-5% A; 10-12 min, 5% A; 12-12.1 min, 5-95% A; and 12.1-15 min, 95% A for column re-equilibration. Mass spectrometric detection of metabolites was performed on Q Exactive(Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with ESI ion source. Simultaneous MS1 and MS/MS (Full MS-ddMS2 mode, data-dependent MS/MS) acquisition was used. The parameters were as follows: sheath gas pressure, 30 arb; aux gas flow, 10 arb; spray voltage, 3.50 kV and - 2.50 kV for ESI(+) and ESI(-), respectively; capillary temperature, 325 C; MS1 range, m/z 100-1000; MS1 resolving power, 70,000 FWHM; number of data dependant scans per cycle, 10; MS/MS resolving power, 17,500 FWHM; normalized collision energy, 30 eV; dynamic exclusion time, automatic.

Raw data were converted to mzXML format using MSConvert in ProteoWizard (v3.0.8789). Converted files were processed with XCMS for feature detection, retention time correction, and alignment. Peaks were identified and annotated using Metlin, MassBank, LipidMaps, mzCloud, and KEGG (http://www.genome.jp/kegg/). Data normalization was performed using the robust LOESS signal correction (QC-RLSC) method to mitigate systematic biases. After normalization, ion peaks with relative standard deviations (RSDs) below a threshold were selected for further analysis to ensure reliability. Metabolite identification was conducted by comparison with authentic standards and reference data. Multivariate analyses and modeling were performed using ropls software. After scaling, models were built using principal component analysis (PCA), partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA). Each model effectively distinguished sample groups. Permutation testing was applied to assess overfitting risk. Descriptive performance was measured using cumulative R2X and R2Y; an ideal model achieves R2X = 1 and R2Y = 1. Predictive performance was assessed via Q2, which should be close to 1 for optimal models. Permutation testing ensured reliability, with R2 and Q2 values from permuted data significantly lower than the original. Using OPLS-DA, significant metabolites were identified based on variable importance in projection (VIP) scores. Metrics including P-values, VIP scores, and fold changes were evaluated. Ultimately, metabolites with a false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted P value < 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg method) and VIP score > 1 were considered statistically significant.
RNA extraction and transcriptome analysis

For each experimental group (F*_T, F*_X, M*_T, M*_X), three independent biological replicates (n = 3) were analyzed. Total RNA was isolated from breast and leg tissue samples using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RNA integrity was evaluated using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies) and agarose gel electrophoresis, while RNA purity was measured with a NanoPhotometer spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Raw sequencing data often contain adapter sequences and low-quality reads; these were removed using Cutadapt (v1.15) to generate high-quality clean data for downstream analysis. Gene expression levels were quantified and normalized to fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM). Differential gene expression analysis was conducted via DESeq (version 1.30.0) with the following criteria: an absolute log2-fold change > 1 and a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P value < 0.05 to control false discovery rate (FDR). Additionally, the Euclidean method was employed to calculate the distances between samples, followed by hierarchical clustering via the complete linkage method.
Validation of RNA-seq data by qRT-PCR

To validate the results of the transcriptome data, 5 DEGs were randomly selected for qRT-PCR analysis. The specific primer sequences are as follows: aldehyde dehydrogenase 7 family member A1 (ALDH7A1, 5 F: cacccattgtccacacagag; R: caatctctgccccacttgtt), adenosine monophosphate deaminase 3 (AMPD3, 5 F: gcagaacttggcaaaatggt; R: tgggattgattgttgcttca), glutathione S-transferase theta 1 (GSTT1, 5 F: acaacatcccgttcgagttc; R: ttagcatgatgccacgagag), fatty acid elongase 1 (ELOVL1, 5 F: cttgtgttgggcatccttct; R: ccctgccatcagaaactcat), myosin light chain 9 (MYL9, 5 F: ggttcattcacgaggaccat; R: ttgtccttagctccgtgctt). Total mRNA from the samples was extracted using the Trizol Kit. cDNA synthesis was then performed according to the manufacturer's instructions using the PrimeScriptTM RT Reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was conducted using the Roche Step One real-time PCR system (Roche, USA). PCR amplification of all samples was performed in triplicate. beta-Actin (5 F: tgcgtgacatcaaggagaag; R: tgccagggtacattgtggta) was used as the normalization control to calculate the relative expression levels.
Statistical analysis and integrative multi-omics analysis

Data are presented as means +- standard errors. Statistical comparisons for phenotypic and targeted omics data were conducted using Student's t-test in SPSS Statistics (v28.0, IBM), with P < 0.05 considered significant. To elucidate the molecular networks regulating carcass characteristics, we systematically integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles. Significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs; llog2FCl >1, P-adj < 0.05 from DESeq2) and significantly different metabolites (SDMs; VIP > 1 from OPLS-DA, P < 0.05) were mapped to KEGG pathways using the KEGG Mapper-Search&Color Pathway tool (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/). Common KEGG pathways significantly enriched (P < 0.05) by both DEGs and SDMs were identified for each comparison group using Fisher's exact test in the clusterProfiler R package (v4.6.2). Pathways meeting this dual-enrichment criterion were designated as key regulatory pathways. Pairwise pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between the abundance levels of SDMs and the expression levels of DEGs within these common pathways, using the cor function in R (v4.3.1). Only gene-metabolite pairs with a strong correlation (lrl >0.8) and statistical significance (P < 0.05) were retained for network construction. Metabolite pathway enrichment analysis, based solely on SDMs, was performed using the Pathway Analysis module of MetaboAnalyst 5.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca) with the Gallus gallus pathway library. Pathways with P < 0.05 from the hypergeometric test and a pathway impact score > 0.1 were considered significantly enriched. Correlation coefficients between metabolites were visualized as heatmaps using the ComplexHeatmap R package (v2.16.0).
Results
Meat quality traits by sex and muscle type

At 20 weeks, male chickens exhibited significantly higher live body weight than females (Fig. 1A). The shear force of both breast and leg muscles was greater in males than in females (P < 0.01) (Fig. 1B). For breast muscles, no significant sex-based differences were observed in drip loss or cooking loss (P > 0.05) (Fig. 1C and D). However, male leg muscles showed lower cooking loss (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1D). Regarding meat color, female leg muscles had higher brightness (L*) (P < 0.05) but lower redness (a*) (P < 0.001) and yellowness (b*) (P < 0.05) compared to males (Fig. 1E and G). In breast muscles, females exhibited lower redness (a*) (P < 0.001) and higher yellowness (b*) (P < 0.05) than males (Fig. 1F and G). Male leg muscles also displayed lower yellowness (P < 0.01) (Fig. 1G). Post-mortem pH (measured at 45 min and 24 h) did not differ significantly between sexes in either muscle type (P > 0.05) (Fig. 1H).

The meat quality traits of breast and leg muscle between female and male chickens (n = 30). A The live body weights of male and female chickens at marketable ages. The shear force (B), drip loss (C), cooking loss (D), L value (E), a value (F), b value (G), pH45min (H), and pH24h (I) were measured. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001

Within the same sex, the shear force of female breast muscle was significantly higher than that of leg muscle (P < 0.05). Cooking loss was lower in breast muscles compared to leg muscles for both females and males (P < 0.05). For males, the L* value of breast muscle was significantly higher, while the a* value was significantly lower than in leg muscle (P < 0.05). In females, both L* and b* values were significantly higher in breast muscle than in leg muscle (P < 0.05). No significant difference was observed in pH at 45 min-24 h between female breast and leg muscles (P > 0.05). However, for females, pH at both time points was significantly higher in leg muscle than in breast muscle (P < 0.05) (Fig.S1).
Metabolic profiles of the breast and leg muscles of female and male chickens
Metabolite classification and PCA/OPLS-DA analysis

To examine the metabolic differences between female and male chickens, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) was performed in both positive and negative ion modes. A total of 6,483 metabolites were identified in the positive ion mode, while 8,358 metabolites were detected in the negative ion mode. These metabolites, including those observed in both modes, were subsequently categorized based on their chemical taxonomy. The analysis revealed that the top five classes among the identified metabolites were carboxylic acids and derivatives (13%), endogenous metabolites: natural products/medicines (11%), organooxygen compounds (9%), benzene and substituted derivatives (8%) and fatty acyls (7%) (Fig. 2A). Amino acids, peptides, and analogs had the highest proportion among the classified subclasses (13%) (Fig. 2B). In the comparison of female and male chicken breast muscles, the PCA accounted for 26.4% of total variance by the first principal component (PC1) and 21.7% by the second principal component (PC2) (Fig. 2A, B). Similarly, for the leg muscles, PCA explained 26.4% (PC1) and 21.7% (PC2) of the total variance (Fig. 2C, D). The PCA score plot revealed that 37.6% of the variation between the breast and leg muscles of male chickens could be explained by two components, whereas 35.2% of the variation between the breast and leg muscles of female chickens could be explained by two components (Fig. 2E and F). The OPLS-DA plots revealed clear distinctions in metabolite profiles across the four comparative groups (Fig. 2G and J). The OPLS-DA models exhibited strong performance, with explained variation (R2Y) and predictive ability (Q2) values both exceeding 0.5 and R2Y values surpassing 0.9. These metrics indicate that the models are robust and suitable for subsequent analysis.

Sex-specific differential metabolites

Using VIP scores from OPLS-DA models, we identified significantly different metabolites (SDMs) with the criteria VIP > 1 and p < 0.05. In the breast muscle, we observed an upregulation of 8 metabolites in male chickens, with a distinct predominance of 25-hydroxycholesterol, 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid and oxidized glutathione. Similarly, in the breast of female chickens, we observed an upregulation of 16 metabolites, prominently featuring pelargonic acid and NAD (Fig. 2K and Table S2). Compared with those in F*_T, a total of 10 metabolites were upregulated in M*_T, with the majority of these upregulated metabolites being pelletierine, N-a-acetylcitrulline and L-valine (Fig. 2L and Table S3). Using the VIP scores obtained from the OPLS-DA models, we identified differentially accumulated metabolites by applying the criteria of VIP > 1 and P < 0.05. This result indicates that carboxylic acids and their derivatives are the predominant differentially abundant metabolite types distinguishing female and male chickens within the same tissue. Interestingly, within the same sex, a greater number of differentially abundant metabolites were identified between the breast and leg muscles. In M*_X, a total of 31 metabolites were differentially upregulated compared with those in M*_T. Conversely, in M*_T, 20 metabolites were differentially upregulated (Fig. 2M; Table S4). The 31 metabolites that were upregulated in M*_X were mainly identified as oxidized glutathione, 1-arachidonoylglycerol, and adenosine diphosphate ribose. On the other hand, the 20 metabolites that were upregulated in M*_T were predominantly categorized as bovinic acid and 13S-hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid. On the other hand, compared with those in F*_T, 34 metabolites were upregulated in F*_X, whereas 19 were upregulated in F*_T (Fig. 2N; Table S5). The 34 upregulated metabolites in F*_X were associated with L-valine, dihydroxyacetone phosphate, gamma-L-glutamyl-D-alanine, glycerophosphocholine and NAD, whereas the 19 upregulated metabolites in F*_T were primarily anserine and thioguanine. These findings indicate that carboxylic acids and their derivatives, fatty acyls, and glycerophospholipids are the primary categories of differentially abundant metabolites when sex and tissue type are compared. The VIP scores were used to pinpoint crucial metabolites showing significant content differences. In the breast muscle of female and male chickens, the top five candidate biomarkers, namely, lysoPA, diethylstilbestrol, D-galactose, erucic acid and gabapentin, were upregulated in males compared with female chickens. Conversely, 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid, aminophenazone, NAD, 25-hydroxycholesterol and myristoleic acid were downregulated in M*_X. In the leg muscle of female chickens, specific compounds such as NAD, norepinephrine, 6,8a-Seco-6,8a-deoxy-5-oxoavermectin ''2b'' aglycone, methyldopa, and prostaglandin H2 were enriched. Conversely, in the leg muscle of male chickens, different compounds, including 1-arachidonoylglycerol, L-valine, p-cresol sulfate, 3-methylhistidine, dopamine, N-acetylputrescine, 4-pyridoxic acid, and N-a-acetylcitrulline, were more enriched. In the comparison of differentially abundant metabolites between M*_X and M*_T, several key metabolites were identified. Notably, oxidized glutathione, 1-arachidonoylglycerol, 13 S-hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid, adenosine diphosphate ribose, and anserine were among the top differentiated metabolites. On the other hand, the five dominant metabolites in M*_T are 12,13-epoxy-9(Z)-tridecenoic acid (12,13-EpOME), undecanoic acid, guanosine monophosphate (GMP), 6-hydroxynicotinic acid, and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. In F*_X, significant metabolites included L-valine, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), and gamma-L-glutamyl-D-alanine. In F*_T, there was an increasing trend for docosapentaenoic acid (22n-3), biotin, oleic acid, and 3'-adenylic acid (3'-AMP).
Pathway enrichment analysis

The biological functions of the differentially abundant metabolites were determined through KEGG pathway analysis via MetaboAnalyst 5.0. In the breast muscle between the female and male chickens, several pathways were significantly enriched (P < 0.05), including the intestinal immune network for IgA production and histidine metabolism (Table S6, Fig. 2O). In the leg muscle between female and male chickens, the differentially abundant metabolites were involved in nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (P < 0.05) (Table S7, Fig. 2P). Regarding the differentially abundant metabolites between M*_X and M*_T, the identified pathways included linoleic acid metabolism, purine metabolism, vascular smooth muscle contraction, the intestinal immune network for IgA production, and galactose metabolism (Table S8, Fig. 2Q). Conversely, the metabolites that varied between F*_X and F*_T were predominantly associated with linoleic acid metabolism, histidine metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation (Table S9, Fig. 2R).
Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between female and male chickens
Transcriptomic profiling and 3DPCA

A total of 42,627,098-48,522,692 raw reads and 40,398,516-45,940,730 clean reads were obtained through transcriptome analysis of each muscle tissue sample (Table S10). The alignment rate of these clean reads to the reference genome varied from 93.17% to 95.30%, with each sample displaying uniquely mapped reads within this range (Table S10). Specifically, the 3DPCA (Three-Dimensional Principal Component Analysis) analysis explained 79% (F*_X vs. M*_X), 67% (F*_T vs. M*_T), 79% (M*_T vs. M*_X), and 81% (F*_T vs. F*_X) of the variability (Fig. 3A-D).

Sex-specific DEGs

We identified 211 upregulated and 166 downregulated DEGs between F*_X and M*_X (Fig. 3E; Table S11). In the DEGs of the top 10 upregulated, growth arrest and DNA damage inducible gamma (GADD45G), protogenin (PRTG), homeobox A1 (HOXA1), nyctalopin, transmembrane protein 86 A (TMEM86A), synaptosome associated protein 47 (SNAP47), bone morphogenetic protein 7 (BMP7), caspase 10 (CASP10), CCAAT/enhancer binding protein delta (CEBPD), and solute carrier family 41 member 3 (SLC41A3) are the gene with the most significant difference. In the DEGs of the top 10 down-regulated, histidine triad nucleotide binding protein W (HINTW), phospholipid phosphatase related 4 (PLPPR4), fucosyltransferase 7 (FUT7), BARX homeobox 2 (BARX2), TNFAIP3 interacting protein 3 (TNIP3), C-C motif chemokine receptor 6 (CCR6), follistatin like 4 (FSTL4), marker of proliferation Ki-67, keratinocyte differentiation factor 1 (KDF1), and RAD51 recombinase are the gene with the most significant difference. The top ten enriched biological processes were sterol biosynthetic process, positive regulation of biological process, cholesterol biosynthetic process, secondary alcohol biosynthetic process, immune system development, system development, cellular response to chemical stimulus, response to organonitrogen compound, cellular response to organic substance, and hemopoiesis (Fig. 3F). KEGG pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment in metabolic pathways, including steroid biosynthesis, histidine metabolism, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, glycerophospholipid metabolism, drug metabolism-cytochrome P450, and fatty acid degradation (Fig. 3G). By comparing the leg muscles of female and male chickens, we identified 486 DEGs, with 172 upregulated and 314 downregulated genes (Fig. 3H; Table S12). In the DEGs of the top 10 upregulated, short stature homeobox 2 (SHOX2), annexin A13 (ANXA13), cysteine and glycine rich protein 3 (CSRP3), 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1E (HTR1E), myosin light chain 3 (MYL3), solute carrier family 10 member 4 (SLC10A4), growth arrest and DNA damage inducible gamma (GADD45G), cochlin (COCH), follicle stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR), and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1 (PCSK1) are the gene with the most significant difference. In the DEGs of the top 10 down-regulated, histidine triad nucleotide binding protein W (HINTW), ubiquitin associated protein 2 (UBAP2), 60 S ribosomal protein L17, retinol binding protein 7 (RBP7), cell death inducing DFFA like effector c (CIDEC), perilipin 1 (PLIN1), joining chain of multimeric IgA and IgM (JCHAIN), myosin VIIA (MYO7A), somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2), and polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 6 (GALNT6) are the gene with the most significant difference. These DEGs were enriched in various functional categories, including immunological memory formation process, cell surface, immunological memory process, myosin complex, cell surface receptor signaling pathway, CNTFR-CLCF1 complex, cellular water homeostasis, embryonic genitalia morphogenesis, extracellular region, and tissue development (Fig. 3I). Additionally, through KEGG analyses, we identified several top pathways that were enriched among the DEGs. These pathways included metabolic pathways, steroid biosynthesis, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, galactose metabolism, fructose and mannose metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, one carbon pool by folate, neomycin, kanamycin and gentamicin biosynthesis, folate biosynthesis, ubiquinone and other terpenoid-quinone biosynthesis, mucin type O-glycan biosynthesis, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, and alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism (Fig. 3J). These results suggest that these pathways play crucial roles in influencing the differences in meat quality between female and male chickens.

passages.text: Tissue-specific DEGs

We also examined differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between these two chicken tissues. A comparison of M*_T and M*_X revealed 652 DEGs whose expression was upregulated and 1236 DEGs whose expression was downregulated (Fig. 3K; Table S13). In the DEGs of the top 10 upregulated, immunoglobulin-like and fibronectin type III domain containing 1, troponin C1 (TNNC1), SIM bHLH transcription factor 2 (SIM2), alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase 2 (AGXT2), FERM domain containing 5 (FRMD5), plakophilin 1 (PKP1), gap junction protein beta 2 (GJB2), gap junction protein beta 6 (GJB6), four and a half LIM domains 2 (FHL2), and apolipoprotein C3(APOC3) are the gene with the most significant difference. In the DEGs of the top 10 down-regulated, myosin light chain 3 (MYL3), myosin light chain 2 (MYL2), phospholamban (PLN), parvalbumin (PVALB), cysteine and glycine rich protein 3 (CSRP3), myoglobin (MB), myosin heavy chain 1 F (MYH1F), myozenin 2 (MYOZ2), potassium voltage-gated channel modifier subfamily F member 1 (KCNF1), glutamate ionotropic receptor NMDA type subunit 2 C (GRIN2C) are the gene with the most significant difference. GO analysis revealed that the upregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in several biological processes and molecular functions, including oxidation-reduction processes, generation of precursor metabolites and energy, energy derivation by oxidation of organic compounds, NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) activity, NADH dehydrogenase (quinone) activity, and phosphate-containing compound metabolic processes (Fig. 3L). KEGG analysis revealed that the majority of the DEGs were associated with metabolic pathways; glycolysis/gluconeogenesis; oxidative phosphorylation; fatty acid degradation; pyruvate metabolism; propanoate metabolism; valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation; the citrate cycle; glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism; cysteine and methionine metabolism; starch and sucrose metabolism; and beta-alanine metabolism (Fig. 3M). Furthermore, in the comparison between F*_T and F*_X, a greater number of DEGs were observed. Specifically, 390 DEGs were upregulated in the breast muscle, whereas 660 DEGs were downregulated (Fig. 3N; Table S14). In the DEGs of the top 10 upregulated, troponin C1, slow skeletal and cardiac type (TNNC1), immunoglobulin-like and fibronectin type III domain containing 1, secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1), SIM bHLH transcription factor 2 (SIM2), FERM domain containing 5 (FRMD5), phospholipid phosphatase related 4 (PLPPR4), myosin heavy chain 1E (MYH1E), alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase 2 (AGXT2), gap junction protein beta 2 (GJB2), cilia and flagella associated protein 44 (CFAP44) are the gene with the most significant difference. In the DEGs of the top 10 down-regulated, homeobox C10 (HOXC10), myosin heavy chain 1 F (MYH1F), parvalbumin (PVALB), phospholamban (PLN), myosin light chain 3 (MYL3), ankyrin repeat domain 2 (ANKRD2), myosin binding protein C (MYBPC1), leiomodin 2 (LMOD2), myosin light chain 2 (MYL2) are the gene with the most significant difference. These DEGs were significantly enriched in myofibril regulation, including small molecule metabolic processes, oxoacid metabolic processes, carboxylic acid metabolic processes, organic acid metabolic processes, monocarboxylic acid metabolic processes, cellular lipid metabolic processes, organophosphate metabolic processes, muscle system processes, contractile fibers, and myofibrils (Fig. 3O). Additionally, KEGG pathway analysis revealed that the DEGs were involved in metabolic pathways; glycolysis/gluconeogenesis; fatty acid degradation; pyruvate metabolism; glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism; propanoate metabolism; and valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation (Fig. 3P). These findings suggest that the DEGs between the breast and leg muscles play crucial roles in determining muscle phenotype.

passages.text: qRT-PCR verification of DEGs

To provide additional evidence for the gene expression profiles recorded at the transcriptome level, the differential expression of 5 selected DEGs like ALDH7A1, AMPD3, GSTT1, ELOVL1, and MYL9 was validated by qRT-PCR. The expression pattern of the selected genes obtained by quantitative Real Time PCR in additional cohort of samples was in agreement with the RNA-seq data, although the magnitude was variable (Fig. S2).
Integrative analysis of the transcriptome and metabolome in the breast and leg muscles of female and male chickens
Integrative pathway and correlation analysis of sex-specific differences in breast muscle

We explored the potential common pathways influencing meat quality by examining the accumulated metabolites and genes with significant differences. When comparing M*_X and F*_X, we identified 10 KEGG pathways that were shared between the transcriptome and metabolome (Fig. 4A). By ranking the pathways on the basis of the number of SDMs/DEGs and their enriched P values, we identified significant pathways between F*_X and M*_X, including oxidative phosphorylation, arginine and proline metabolism, histidine metabolism, beta-alanine metabolism, glutathione metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, ether lipid metabolism, drug metabolism-other enzymes, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, and ferroptosis (Fig. 4B).

F*_X: the breast muscle of female chicken, F*_T: the leg muscle of female chicken, M*_T: the leg muscle of male chicken, M*_X: the breast muscle of male chicken

To gain further insight into the associations between the metabolic and transcriptomic profiles of the breast tissue of female and male chickens, we conducted a correlation analysis of the differentially expressed genes and differentially abundant metabolites. Figure 4C illustrates the significant correlation between 2418 gene-metabolite pairs, where 1022 pairs were positively correlated and 1396 pairs were negatively correlated (Table S15). Among the notable metabolites, anserine, oxidized glutathione, 1-methylhistidine, and NAD were found to interact with most of the DEGs (Table S15). Additionally, we performed a network analysis focusing on the genes and metabolites that participate in shared pathways, which revealed critical factors affecting meat quality between F*_X and M*_X (Fig. 4D). The Pearson method was employed to evaluate the correlation between SDMs and DEGs, with a specific focus on pairs exhibiting correlation coefficients greater than 0.8 and P-values less than 0.05, which were considered to be strongly correlated. Figure 4D shows that the differentially accumulated metabolites and DEGs were involved primarily in amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism and energy metabolism. Specifically, in amino acid metabolism, 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid was significantly positively correlated with ALDH7A1 and ASPA and negatively correlated with ATP5F1AW, which were enriched in arginine and proline metabolism; 1-Methylhistidine was positively correlated with ATP5F1AW and ELOVL1 and negatively correlated with CHAC1, GSTT1, GPCPD1 and ALDH7A1, which were enriched in histidine metabolism; Anserine was positively correlated with CHAC1, GSTT1, GPCPD1 and ALDH7A1 and negatively correlated with ATP5F1AW, which were enriched in beta-alanine metabolism; and oxidized glutathione was positively correlated with CHAC1, ALDH7A1, GPCPD1 and GSTT1 and negatively correlated with ATP5F1AW, which were enriched in glutathione metabolism (Fig. 4D). In lipid metabolism, glycerophosphocholine was significantly positively correlated with ATP5F1AW and negatively correlated with ALDH7A1 and GPCPD1, which are enriched in glycerophospholipid metabolism. Erucic acid was positively correlated with GPCPD1 and CHAC1, which are enriched in the biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids (Fig. 4D). In energy metabolism, NAD was significantly positively correlated with ATP5F1AW and negatively correlated with CHAC1, GPCPD1, ALDH7A1, ELOVL1 and GSTT1, which were enriched in oxidative phosphorylation (Fig. 4D).
Integrative pathway and correlation analysis of sex-specific differences in leg muscle

Similarly, in the comparison between F*_T and M*_T, we identified 11 common KEGG pathways (Fig. 4E), namely, ABC transporters; adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes; arginine biosynthesis; fructose and mannose metabolism; gap junction; neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction; nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism; oxidative phosphorylation; phenylalanine metabolism; tyrosine metabolism; and vascular smooth muscle contraction (Fig. 4F). Correlation analysis between differentially abundant metabolites and DEGs revealed 2442 significantly correlated gene-metabolite pairs, with 1316 showing positive correlations and 1126 showing negative correlations (Fig. 4G; Table S16). L-valine, 1-arachidonoylglycerol, N-a-acetylcitrulline, mannitol, and glycerophosphocholine were found to interact with most of the DEGs (Table S16). We conducted network analysis of the genes and metabolites involved in common pathways, which are involved primarily in amino acid metabolism, energy metabolism and membrane transport. (Fig. 4H). In amino acid metabolism, trans-3-hydroxycinnamate was significantly positively correlated with ABCG2, ATP5A1Z, AKR1B10, BDKRB1, CHRNA6, HTR1E, COX7C and ATP6V1C2 and negatively correlated with ASS1 and HK2, which are enriched in phenylalanine metabolism. Norepinephrine was positively correlated with ATP5I, MYL9, HPD and FSHR and negatively correlated with PTGFR, which is enriched in tyrosine metabolism. N-a-acetylcitrulline was positively correlated with CHRNA6, MYL9, ABCB11, ATP6V1C2, MYL3, COX7C, ATP5I, and ABCG2. In energy metabolism, NAD was significantly positively correlated with HK2, SSTR2 and PTGFR and negatively correlated with PFKFB3, COX7C and ATP5A1Z, which are enriched in oxidative phosphorylation (Fig. 4H). In terms of membrane transport, L-valine was positively correlated with FSHR, HPD, ABCG2, PFKFB3, ATP5A1Z, ATP5I and COX7C and negatively correlated with AKR1B10, PTGFR, HK2, CREB5, ASS1, NMRK2 and P2RX7, which were enriched with ABC transporters (Fig. 4H).
Sex-specific regulatory pathways

The integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic data between female and male chickens revealed that the differentially accumulated metabolites and DEGs were involved primarily in histidine metabolism and nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (Fig. 5). Specifically, in terms of histidine metabolism, MAOA showed increased accumulation, and ALDH7A1 and ASPA showed decreased accumulation in female chickens, resulting in increased flavor metabolites, such as anserine (Fig. 5). Two metabolites also differentially accumulated during nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism. NAD and niacinamide were upregulated in male chickens, and NMRK2 exhibited decreased accumulation in male chickens (Fig. 5). Therefore, histidine metabolism and nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism were differentially regulated between female and male chickens.
