passages.text: From pathogenesis to therapeutic targeting: new insight into TAM receptors in rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a systemic autoimmune disorder driven by chronic joint inflammation and progressive tissue damage, is orchestrated by a complex interplay of immune cells and signaling pathways. Among these, the TAM receptor family, comprising Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK, has emerged as a critical regulator of immune homeostasis and inflammatory resolution. Activation of TAM receptors by their cognate ligands helps restore tissue integrity through key mechanisms including the suppression of innate immune cell activation, enhancement of apoptotic cells (ACs) clearance, and promotion of tissue repair. Given these multifaceted roles, the TAM signaling pathway presents a compelling therapeutic target for RA. This review systematically delineates the biological rationale for targeting TAM receptors in RA, explores their potential as diagnostic biomarkers, and evaluates the current landscape of TAM-directed therapeutics. Ultimately, targeting the TAM axis offers a promising avenue to refine clinical management strategies for RA.
Introduction

RA is an autoimmune and inflammatory disease that causes chronic, persistent inflammation, synovial cell hyperplasia, and joint destruction. This disease typically presents with pain, swelling, and stiffness in synovial joints. The pathogenesis of RA involves complex interactions between immune cells and joint cells, where autoimmune cells produce a variety of cytokines, chemokines, and other local inflammatory mediators. These substances drive the inflammatory and destructive processes in synovial joints. Additionally, fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS), chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts also contribute to the secretion of inflammatory factors and the transduction of related signaling pathways, further exacerbating the progression of the disease.

The TAM receptors are broadly expressed throughout the body and play roles in processes such as exocytosis, immune response, and maintaining inflammation balance. Numerous studies have highlighted the critical role of TAM receptors in managing the immune imbalance observed in RA. TAM receptors regulate inflammatory cascades and mediate the phagocytosis of ACs, thus helping to prevent autoimmune responses. In TAM-deficient mice, spontaneous chronic inflammation and autoimmune phenomena have been observed, which may serve as clinical precursors to RA, including conditions like bone marrow edema. Among the TAM receptors, Axl and MerTK are known to have protective effects in RA, while Tyro3 is suggested to exacerbate inflammation and joint destruction, thereby facilitating the progression of the disease. In this review, we will explore the role of TAM receptors in regulating immunity and inflammation, its impact on bone homeostasis and cartilage destruction, and its association with intestinal inflammation and the improvement of RA complications. This discussion will underscore the potential of TAM receptors as a therapeutic target for RA.
Structure and function of the TAM receptor family and their ligands

The TAM family is characterized by a single hydrophobic transmembrane domain containing a highly conserved KW(I/L)A(I/L)ES consensus sequence within the intracellular region of the tyrosine kinase catalytic domain. Each receptor features an extracellular domain composed of two immunoglobulin-like (IgL) repeats and two type III fibronectin (FNIII) repeats. The primary ligands for TAM receptors are two homologous proteins: Growth Arrest-Specific Protein 6 (Gas6) and Protein S (Pros1). Both are synthesized via a vitamin K-dependent process and share a similar domain structure. This includes an N-terminal gamma-carboxyglutamic acid domain that facilitates calcium-dependent binding to the negatively charged phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), four epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like repeats, and a C-terminal steroid hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) domain. Gas6 is expressed in a variety of cell types such as vascular endothelial cells, platelets, immune cells, and astrocytes. In contrast, Pros1 expression is predominantly observed in neurons, vascular endothelial cells, platelets, Sertoli cells, retinal pigment epithelial cells, and osteoblasts.

Ligand binding induces TAM receptor dimerization, trans-autophosphorylation, and initiation of downstream signaling. The activation by Gas6 and Pros1 depends on vitamin K-mediated gamma-carboxylation of their Gla domains. Gas6 binds all three TAM receptors with highest affinity for Axl, while Pros1 activates Tyro3 and MerTK but not Axl. Notably, PtdSer exposure enhances ligand-receptor binding and amplifies TAM signaling, with Gas6 and Pros1 acting as molecular bridges between PtdSer and the receptors.

Upon activation, TAM receptors engage multiple downstream pathways, including JAK/STAT, PI3K/AKT, NF-kappaB, RAS/RAF, SRC, VAV1/RAC, and BCL-2, which collectively regulate immune cell survival, proliferation, migration, phagocytosis, and anti-inflammatory responses. For example, MerTK activation via the PI3K/AKT pathway suppresses LTA-induced TNF-alpha and IL-6 production, and TAM signaling broadly dampens toll-like receptor (TLR)-driven MAPK and NF-kappaB activation. Specifically, MerTK triggered by apoptotic cells selectively inhibits LPS-induced NF-kappaB signaling, highlighting its role in restraining inflammation. Moreover, TAM receptors trigger the MAPK cascade reaction by regulating the RAS/RAF pathway, driving cell proliferation; SRC kinase enhances cell migration ability and phagocytic function of immune cells by directly recruiting and activating the intracellular domain of TAM receptors; while the VAV1/RAC pathway regulates the process of cytoskeletal reorganization through the phosphorylation and membrane localization of VAV1 induced by TAM signaling. TAM receptors also promote proliferation via RAS/RAF/MAPK, modulate cytoskeletal dynamics through VAV1/RAC, and enhance phagocytosis and migration via SRC kinase. In addition, TAM signaling influences apoptotic thresholds by regulating BCL-2 family members (Fig. 1).
TAM structure and activation mechanisms.

Gas6 is expressed in vascular endothelial cells, platelets, immune cells, and astrocytes. Pros1 is found in neuronal cells, vascular endothelial cells, platelets, supporting cells, retinal pigment epithelial cells, and osteoblasts. The TAM receptor family includes Axl, MerTK, and Tyro3, all sharing a common structure with two IgL repeats and two type III fibronectin (FNIII) repeats in the extracellular domain. Gas6 and Pros1, the main ligands, contain a Gla domain, four epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like domains, and two immunoglobulin (LG)-like domains. Gas6 activates all three TAM kinases but binds most strongly to Axl. Pros1 specifically activates Tyro3 and MerTK. After phosphorylation, TAM receptors trigger signaling pathways such as Janus Kinase/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (JAK/STAT), Nuclear Factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-kappaB), Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase/AKT murine thymoma viral oncogene homolog (PI3K/AKT), Rat Sarcoma virus oncogene/Rapidly Accelerated Fibrosarcoma kinase (RAS/RAF), Sarcoma rous carcinoma virus oncogene homolog (SRC), Vav Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factor 1/RAS-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate (VAV1/RAC), and B-Cell Lymphoma-2 (BCL-2). These pathways regulate immune cell proliferation, survival, migration, invasion, anti-apoptosis, immunosuppression, and anti-inflammatory responses
Dysregulation of TAM receptors expression in RA

In RA, pathogenic immune responses are driven by multiple dysregulated cell types: T cells recruit inflammatory cells, activated macrophages accumulate and secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, autoreactive B cells expand and produce autoantibodies, and dendritic cells (DCs) efficiently present antigens to activate pro-inflammatory T cells. Concurrently, resident cells within the joint, including osteoblasts, osteoclasts, chondrocytes, and synovial cells, undergo inflammatory activation and contribute to tissue damage. The abnormal expression of TAM receptors in these cells suggests their involvement in RA pathogenesis.

MerTK demonstrates significant upregulation in RA. This receptor is highly expressed on immunosuppressive myeloid cells, with markedly elevated levels of membrane-bound MerTK (mMerTK) observed on macrophages from RA patients. Synovial tissues also show increased mMerTK expression. Tyro3 exhibits distinct dysregulation patterns in RA. MTyro3 is significantly elevated in RA synovial tissues, and its increased expression on CD14+CD16- monocytes may provide important signals for osteoclast differentiation. Axl displays a more complex expression profile. This receptor is primarily localized to vascular endothelial cells and M2-like macrophages in synovial tissues. In ankle joints, mAxl appears to play a crucial role in suppressing arthritis. However, mAxl expression is reduced on DCs, potentially contributing to RA pathogenesis.

Beyond membrane-bound receptors, soluble forms of TAM receptors (sTAM) also show significant alterations in RA. The extracellular domains of Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK can be cleaved by metalloproteinases to generate soluble receptors. In RA synovial fluid, sTyro3, sAxl, and sMerTK are all significantly elevated, further confirming the close association between TAM receptor dysregulation and RA pathology.
TAM receptor family: critical role in immune regulation and inflammatory response

TAM receptors are key pleiotropic inhibitors in the immune system, expressed on and exerting critical functions in various immune cells, including T cells, macrophages, DCs, natural killer (NK) cells, and neutrophils. TAM receptors provide an essential inhibitory feedback mechanism that safeguards the resolution of inflammation and promotes tissue repair processes following the initiation of adaptive immune responses. Blocking TAM signaling results in severe defects in the clearance of ACs, exacerbates systemic inflammation, and induces overactivation of the immune system, thereby contributing to the onset and progression of RA (Fig. 2).
Role of TAM receptors in immune regulation in RA.

TAM receptors regulate immunity by modulating various immune cells. In T cells, Axl and Tyro3 inhibit survival and function, while MerTK suppresses proliferation and activity to alleviate autoimmune responses. TAM signaling promotes macrophage polarization to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype and enhances phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, with MerTK playing a key role in resolving inflammation. TAM receptors also limit TLR signaling in dendritic cells (DCs), suppress autoimmunity, regulate NK cell differentiation and activation to prevent tissue damage, and control Fc receptors (FcgammaR) and C5a receptor (C5aR) expression in neutrophils to reduce RA-related inflammation and joint damage. Additionally, MerTK inhibits B cell proliferation, and Axl mediates mast cell adhesion changes to regulate differentiation and inflammation
TAM signaling in T lymphocytes

T cells play a central role in RA pathogenesis by recognizing antigens, secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines, and contributing to tissue damage. They are broadly divided into CD4+ helper T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. In humans, MerTK is expressed on activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells following T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation, whereas Axl is undetectable and Tyro3 is expressed at low levels. MerTK upregulation enhances T cell proliferation, indicating its direct role in promoting T cell expansion. However, TAM receptor expression and function differ between humans and mice. In murine CD4+ regulatory T cells, both Axl and MerTK are constitutively expressed. Moreover, MerTK inhibition in mice does not directly impair T cell function but indirectly reduces programmed death (PD)-1 expression on T cells by modulating DCs and macrophages.

Among CD4+ T cell subsets, Tyro3 specifically restrains type 2 helper T (Th2) responses. In a model of allergic airway inflammation, Tyro3-/- mice exhibited enhanced Th2 reactivity, and IL-4, induced Pros1 was shown to act as a Tyro3 ligand that limits Th2 cytokine production (e.g., IL-13) while suppressing interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) secretion. This Pros1/Tyro3 axis also activates DCs, forming a feedback loop that fine-tunes DCs-T cell crosstalk. In the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model, Gas6 overexpression was associated with reduced CD4+ T cell numbers, suggesting a role in limiting CD4+ T cell survival. Additionally, Axl and MerTK jointly constrain Th1 responses; CD4+ T cells from Axl/MerTK double-knockout mice produce more IFN-gamma, which may exacerbate RA by enhancing Th1-driven immunity.

In CD8+ T cells, TAM receptors modulate function through both direct and indirect mechanisms. In breast cancer models, tumor-derived Axl activation impairs DCs maturation and major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-I presentation via colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) and C-C motif chemokine ligand 3, thereby inhibiting CD8+ T cell activity. Axl inhibition restores MHC-I expression and enhances IFN-gamma production, indirectly supporting CD8+ T cell function. Separately, TCR activation in CD8+ T cells enables Pros1/MerTK signaling, which promotes proliferation and enhances the release of effector molecules such as IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand (CXCL) 10, and IL-7. Thus, tumors exploit both the Axl pathway in DCs and the Pros1/MerTK axis in T cells to bidirectionally control CD8+ T cell activity and abundance.
TAM signaling in macrophages

Macrophages play a central role in the pathogenesis of RA, driving synovitis through cytokine secretion, antigen presentation, and disruption of tissue homeostasis. Their polarization state:broadly classified as pro-inflammatory M1 or anti-inflammatory M2:is critically influenced by TAM receptor signaling, with MerTK in particular promoting the transition from M1 to M2 phenotypes and enhancing phagocytic function.

A key function of TAM receptors in macrophages is the facilitation of ACs clearance. PtdSer exposed on ACs serves as a primary "eat-me" signal, which is recognized by TAM ligands Gas6 and Pros1, thereby bridging ACs to TAM receptors on macrophages. Upon engagement, MerTK activation triggers VAV1 phosphorylation and subsequent cytoskeletal remodeling via Ras Homolog (RHO)/CDC42/RAC pathways, enabling efficient phagocytosis. Under steady-state conditions, MerTK is the dominant receptor for homeostatic ACs clearance, whereas Axl contributes predominantly during inflammatory resolution. Tyro3, by contrast, is minimally expressed in macrophages. Beyond efferocytosis, TAM receptors temper inflammation through multiple mechanisms. Axl can suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1beta maturation, while MerTK is essential for limiting LPS-induced inflammatory responses; its deletion leads to dysregulated cytokine production and increased susceptibility to endotoxic shock. MerTK also modulates inflammation via the STAT1/SOCS pathway, with PI3K/AKT serving as a central node downstream of TAM receptors in regulating macrophage polarization and activation.

Polarization represents another key level of TAM-mediated immunoregulation. MerTK generally suppresses M1 polarization and promotes an M2-like, tissue-reparative phenotype. Following efferocytosis, TAM-stimulated macrophages upregulate PD-L1/PD-L2, reinforcing an immunosuppressive microenvironment. The roles of Axl and Tyro3 in polarization are context-dependent. Tyro3 has been shown to inhibit M1 polarization in mouse peritoneal and tumor-associated macrophages. Axl exhibits dual activity: it supports M2 polarization in some settings, yet in triple-negative breast cancer models, Axl inhibition reduces M1-associated factors such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CSF1, suggesting its function may vary with the immune milieu.
TAM signaling in DCs

DCs are essential antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that initiate and regulate T cell responses, playing a critical role in the balance between immunity and tolerance in RA. TAM signaling serves as a key modulator of DCs activation, restraining excessive immune responses. Mice lacking TAM receptors exhibit hyperactive DCs that enhance lymphocyte proliferation and promote autoimmunity.

Among TAM receptors, Axl acts as a feedback inhibitor of TLR signaling. Type I interferon-induced Axl expression activates SOCS1 and SOCS3, which suppress TLR-triggered pro-inflammatory cytokine production and limit DCs activation. Consistent with this, Axl-/- DCs show enhanced MHC class II expression and elevated IL-6 and TNF-alpha secretion upon TLR stimulation. Tyro3 contributes to the modulation of type 2 immunity. In PD-L2+ DCs, Tyro3 deficiency enhances the production of type 2 chemokines and co-stimulatory molecules, amplifying Th2 responses through DCs-T cell crosstalk. MerTK also negatively regulates DCs function, primarily through engagement with ACs. MerTK signaling blunts NF-kappaB and PI3K/AKT pathways, inhibiting DCs maturation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Furthermore, MerTK activation by ACs impairs LPS-induced maturation and reduces antigen presentation capacity, promoting DCs tolerance. These findings collectively underscore the role of TAM receptors in maintaining DCs homeostasis and restraining aberrant activation in RA.
TAM signaling in NK cells

NK cells are innate effector lymphocytes that eliminate abnormal cells through cytokine secretion and direct cytotoxicity. TAM receptors, Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK, are expressed on NK cells and modulate their development and function, with Axl playing a particularly central role.

The Gas6/Axl axis critically promotes NK cells maturation. Gas6 binding activates Axl and induces STAT5 phosphorylation, which enhances IL-15Ralpha expression and synergistically drives NK cell differentiation. In Axl-/- mice, NK cell development is impaired, showing reduced maturation, diminished cytotoxicity, and fewer mature NK cells in the bone marrow. Similarly, Axl inhibition in human NK precursor cells attenuates IL-15/STAT5 signaling and T-bet expression, compromising their differentiation.

Functionally, Axl exerts bidirectional effects on NK cells activity. It shares downstream signaling components with IL-15, including PI3K/AKT and ERK1/2; in the absence of Axl, IL-15 fails to fully activate these pathways. Moreover, under IL-15 stimulation, pretreatment with type I IFN leads to reduced secretion of type II IFN (e.g.,IFN-gamma) in NK cells, which correlates with the upregulation of Axl expression on NK cells. This indicates that Axl may negatively regulate NK cells function, particularly IFN-gamma production. Blocking Gas6 enhances NK cell activation, yet Axl expression on mature human NK cells remains debated, as it declines during in vitro differentiation. Despite its predominantly inhibitory role, Axl can exhibit bidirectional regulatory effects on NK cells function in specific microenvironments. For example, Kim et al. demonstrated that activating anti-Axl antibodies or recombinant Gas6 specifically upregulates the expression of mature NK cell-specific receptors (e.g., Lymphocyte Antigen (Ly) 49 A, Ly49G2, Ly49C/F/I, Natural Killer Group (NKG) 2 A/C/E and NK cell-related genes (e.g., IL-2Rbeta, perforin, IL-15Ralpha, IFN-gamma), thereby enhancing NK cells cytotoxicity.

Unlike Axl, Tyro3 is not constitutively expressed on NK cells but can be acquired from targeted cells via trogocytosis. Tyro3+ NK cells exhibit heightened cytotoxicity, IFN-gamma production, and expression of activation markers such as CD25, CD69, and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand. Mechanistically, TAM receptors are substrates of the E3 ubiquitin ligase casitas B-lineage lymphoma-b (Cbl-b), which negatively regulates NK cells function. Tyro3 is particularly susceptible to Cbl-b-mediated ubiquitination, and TAM signaling may also suppress NK cells activation by promoting linker for activation of T cells 1 (LAT1) degradation through Cbl-b phosphorylation.
TAM signaling in neutrophils

In RA, neutrophils contribute to joint inflammation and tissue damage by activating other immune cells. TAM receptors modulate neutrophil-driven inflammation through the regulation of Fcgamma receptors (FcgammaRs), C5a receptor (C5aR), and chemokine signaling.

Functionally, TAM receptors exert opposing roles in RA pathogenesis: Axl and MerTK suppress inflammation and attenuate arthritis severity, whereas Tyro3 promotes inflammatory responses and exacerbates disease. These differential effects are linked to their distinct influences on cytokine production and receptor expression in neutrophils. Studies using the K/BxN-STIA model have demonstrated that FcgammaRs play a critical role in arthritis development; specifically, FcgammaRI, FcgammaRII, and FcgammaRIV promote arthritis onset, while FcgammaRIIB inhibits arthritis progression. Notably, deficiencies in Axl and MerTK do not affect the expression of FcgammaRs or C5aR on neutrophils, whereas Tyro3 deficiency significantly downregulates the expression of FcgammaRI, FcgammaRIII, and FcgammaRIV in neutrophils. The immune function of Tyro3 in neutrophils is dependent on the expression of membrane-bound FcgammaRs, which enhances inflammation and increases arthritis severity. Additionally, Tyro3 upregulates the expression of C5aR in neutrophils, potentially regulating antibody-induced arthritis via complement-mediated pathways. In contrast, Axl and MerTK selectively regulate the secretion of chemokine CXCL2, thereby inhibiting neutrophil infiltration and reducing arthritis severity.
TAM signaling in other immune cells

B cells contribute to RA pathogenesis through autoantibody production, antigen presentation, and cytokine secretion. Among TAM receptors, activated B cells express MerTK but not Axl or Tyro3. MerTK signaling suppresses B cell proliferation and limits autoreactive B cell activation. In MerTK-deficient mice, marginal zone B cell numbers increase twofold, and B cell pathogenicity is significantly reduced. MerTK may also promote tolerance in autoreactive B cells by modulating cytokine secretion or attenuating antigen presentation.

Mast cells promote synovitis, cartilage damage, and bone remodeling in RA through the release of inflammatory mediators. Axl is expressed on mast cells and supports their aggregation upon IFN-alpha stimulation, suggesting a role in cell adhesion and inflammatory differentiation. The functions of Tyro3 and MerTK in mast cells, however, remain largely uncharacterized.
TAM receptor family: key role in local joint tissue destruction

The TAM receptor family contributes to RA progression not only by modulating systemic inflammation but also through direct involvement in joint tissue destruction. In RA, bone metabolism is dysregulated, with enhanced osteoclast-driven resorption and suppressed osteoblast-mediated formation. TAM receptors regulate this balance, with Tyro3 promoting bone erosion and Axl/MerTK exerting protective effects (Fig. 3). Similarly, in cartilage, which has limited regenerative capacity, Axl and MerTK support chondrocyte differentiation and mitigate degeneration. Within the synovium, TAM receptors correlate negatively with pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and influence FLS proliferation, synovial macrophage dynamics, and angiogenesis, collectively shaping joint homeostasis (Fig. 4).
TAM receptors in RA-associated bone homeostasis

In osteoblasts, Axl promotes proliferation and survival via Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase/AKT murine thymoma viral oncogene homolog (PI3K/AKT) but inhibits mineralization. Tyro3 suppresses Ras Homolog Family Member A (RHOA) signaling, promoting cytoskeletal remodeling, differentiation, and mineralization. MerTK induces RHOA-ROCK signaling, negatively regulating WNT signaling pathway (WNT) and IGF-1 pathways, and inhibiting differentiation and mineralization. In osteoclasts, Axl expression in precursors (CD14+CD16-) upregulates Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1 (MCP-1) to promote differentiation. Gas6 activates Tyro3 phosphorylation and Extracellular Signal-Regulated Kinase (ERK) signaling, enhancing differentiation and bone resorption. MerTK induces RHOA signaling in precursors, further promoting differentiation and migration
TAM signaling in synovium ecosystem

The TAM receptor family exhibits dual regulatory effects on the functions of chondrocytes and synovial cells. In chondrocytes, Gas6 inhibits IGF-I-induced proliferation by suppressing Extracellular Signal-Regulated Kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) activation while promoting differentiation. Axl and MerTK exert stage-specific regulation during early and late chondrocyte differentiation, respectively. For synovial cells, TAM receptors modulate the behavior of Fibroblast-like Synoviocytes (FLS), synovial macrophages, and vascular endothelial cells. Gas6-Tyro3 signaling promotes FLS proliferation and synovial hyperplasia, thereby exacerbating inflammation and joint damage. Conversely, MerTK suppresses synovial macrophage proliferation and induces apoptosis, thus exerting anti-inflammatory effects. Moreover, Axl enhances Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)-dependent angiogenesis in the synovium, contributing to pathological neovascularization
TAM receptors in RA-associated bone homeostasis
TAM signaling in osteoblasts

Osteoblasts promote bone formation and mineralization, contribute to the dynamic balance of bone remodeling, and regulate osteoclast differentiation and activity through the secretion of receptor activator of NF-kappaB Ligand (RANKL) and osteoprotegerin (OPG), thereby maintaining bone homeostasis. The Tyro3/Axl/MerTK signaling pathway differentially regulates osteoblast differentiation and function through cell-specific mechanisms and cross-talk. MerTK disrupts osteoblast cytoskeletal organization by inducing cell contraction and stress fiber formation, thereby impairing osteoblast differentiation and suppressing bone formation, ultimately exerting a negative regulatory role in physiological bone remodeling. In pathological conditions such as cancer-induced bone loss, Pros1 activates MerTK on osteoblasts, thereby exacerbating the suppression of bone formation and accelerating bone loss. Notably, the Pros1/MerTK signaling axis negatively regulates osteoblast differentiation via the VAV2-RHOA-ROCK pathway, enhancing cellular contractility and motility. In contrast, Tyro3 antagonizes this effect and functions as a positive regulator of osteoblast activity. Upon activation, Tyro3 directly suppresses the VAV2-RHOA-ROCK pathway, reduces osteoblast migration, and promotes terminal differentiation and matrix mineralization. Under pathological conditions, Tyro3 exerts a protective role in bone homeostasis. In breast cancer bone metastasis models, loss of osteoblast-specific Tyro3 exacerbates tumor-induced bone destruction, whereas its presence mitigates excessive bone resorption by promoting osteoblast differentiation. Axl is capable of promoting bone nodule formation, activating the PI3K/AKT pathway, and inhibiting glycoprotease signaling. Given the well-established role of PI3K/AKT in supporting osteoblast proliferation, survival, and differentiation, Axl is hypothesized to enhance these processes in early-stage osteoblasts. However, its function remains controversial: emerging evidence demonstrates that Axl can inhibit matrix mineralization and impair osteoblast function in mature cells. This dual and stage-dependent role may stem from differential signaling outcomes across osteoblast lineage stages, Axl drives proliferation and survival in osteoprogenitor cells through PI3K/AKT, but suppresses mineralization in mature osteoblasts. This functional switch may be attributed to shifts in intracellular signaling priorities, such as cross-regulation between PI3K/AKT and WNT pathways.
TAM signaling in osteoclasts

Osteoclasts are the primary cells responsible for bone resorption and work in concert with osteoblasts to maintain skeletal homeostasis. In RA, CD14+CD16- monocytes, which serve as the primary osteoclast precursors, exhibit upregulated surface expression of Tyro3. The synovial fluid of RA patients also contains markedly elevated levels of soluble Tyro3 (sTyro3) compared to osteoarthritis patients, resulting from ADAM17-mediated shedding of membrane-bound Tyro3.Functioning as a decoy receptor, sTyro3 competitively binds Gas6 to modulate ligand availability and has been shown to directly enhance the formation of TRAP+ osteoclasts in vitro. The critical role of Tyro3 is further underscored by studies in Tyro3-/- mice, which display increased bone mass, reduced synovial hyperplasia, decreased osteoclast numbers, and attenuated bone destruction. Mechanistically, Gas6-induced activation of Tyro3 promotes receptor phosphorylation and activates the ERK signaling pathway, thereby driving osteoclastogenesis and enhancing the bone-resorptive capacity of mature osteoclasts. MerTK, another key TAM receptor, is similarly implicated in RA pathogenesis. Elevated levels of soluble MerTK (sMerTK) in RA synovial fluid contribute to osteoclast differentiation and migration. sMerTK interacts with the RANKL/RANK/OPG axis, and pharmacological inhibition of MerTK with agents such as the dual MerTK/FLT3 inhibitor MRX-2843 suppresses osteoclast formation, improves bone repair coupling, and promotes bone regeneration and mineralization. Axl, expressed on osteoclast precursors, facilitates osteoclast differentiation by upregulating monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), a key regulator of cell fusion. Beyond its role in resorption, Axl participates in osteoclast-osteoblast coupling: osteoclast-derived RANK-enriched extracellular vesicles activate osteoblasts via Axl-dependent reverse signaling, thereby stimulating bone formation. Consequently, inhibition of the Axl pathway, for example, with the selective inhibitor Bemcentinib, effectively blocks osteoclast differentiation. This effect is potentially mediated through suppression of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade and downregulation of multidrug resistance genes, which collectively impair precursor cell survival and fusion.
TAM receptors in RA-associated cartilage damage
TAM signaling in chondrocytes

In RA, chondrocytes play a dual role: they are both targets of inflammatory mediators, leading to cellular dysfunction, and effector cells that directly or indirectly contribute to joint damage. The expression and functional significance of TAM receptors in these cells have been increasingly elucidated. Loeser et al. confirmed the presence of Gas6 and Axl in human cartilage through immunohistochemical staining and demonstrated their mRNA and protein expression in cultured human chondrocytes. Axl participates in an autocrine signaling pathway within cartilage, promoting chondrocyte proliferation and survival, suggesting a potentially protective role in the arthritic context. Functionally, Gas6 exhibits a complex regulatory profile. It inhibits insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I)-stimulated proliferation of growth plate chondrocytes by attenuating ERK1/2 activation, while simultaneously promoting chondrocyte differentiation.This activity of Gas6 is stage-dependent, a phenomenon attributed to the distinct expression patterns and roles of its receptors, Axl and MerTK, during chondrocyte maturation. Analysis of an in vitro chondrogenesis model revealed that Gas6 suppresses early differentiation markers (e.g., type II collagen and aggrecan) within the first few days, an effect mediated primarily by Axl. In contrast, during later developmental stages, the interaction between Gas6 and MerTK appears to facilitate terminal differentiation. Thus, the differential expression of Axl and MerTK finely modulates the dual functions of Gas6, with Axl exerting influence in the early phase and MerTK supporting later maturation stages.
TAM signaling in synovium ecosystem

TAM receptors collectively regulate synovial biology through distinct cellular pathways. Gas6 binding to Tyro3 induces FLS proliferation; MerTK activation inhibits synovial macrophage expansion and promotes their apoptosis; and Axl functions as a positive regulator of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to stimulate angiogenesis.

FLS mediate joint destruction by secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-6, and IL-18, which recruit immune cells and promote bone erosion. In RA, Tyro3 is specifically overexpressed in FLS, where it drives cellular proliferation and contributes to synovial hyperplasia. Studies using the K/BxN serum transfer arthritis model demonstrate that Tyro3 signaling not only amplifies intra-articular inflammation but also disrupts immune cell homeostasis. Notably, inhibiting Tyro3 significantly reduces the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha in both human RA-derived FLS and experimental models, confirming its central role in synovitis.

MerTK serves as a key marker of synovial macrophages, particularly in the CD206+ subpopulation that is enriched during remission and in healthy joints. Gas6 produced by sublining FLS helps maintain the homeostasis of MerTK+ macrophages in the lining layer. However, TLR4-activated FLS can inhibit the protective shedding of sMerTK, thereby attenuating its anti-inflammatory effects in RA. Reciprocally, macrophage-expressed MerTK suppresses the pro-inflammatory function of FLS, establishing a bidirectional regulatory loop. The spatial distribution of TAM receptors within the synovium is precisely regulated. Axl localizes to CD55-positive lining layer FLS and CD68-positive macrophages, whereas MerTK exhibits specific high expression in CD68-positive macrophages. In the K/BxN mouse model, Axl expression in synovial lining macrophages contributes to a physical barrier within the joint cavity; disruption of this barrier is associated with inflammatory initiation This joint-protective expression of Axl in the ankle synovium is regulated by TGF-beta1, and its deficiency specifically exacerbates ankle arthritis without significantly affecting knee joints. Meanwhile, MerTK activation controls synovial inflammation by inhibiting macrophage proliferation and inducing apoptosis through regulation of apoptotic signaling pathways.

Within the inflammatory synovial microenvironment, the Gas6/Axl signaling axis supports pathological vascular persistence. Gas6 promotes the survival of activated endothelial cells and other Axl+ cells under hypoxic and oxidative stress conditions, thereby maintaining abnormal vascular networks in the synovium. Axl is highly expressed in a vascular-specific pattern in RA synovial tissues, primarily localized to vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells. Functional studies confirm that Axl enhances angiogenesis by enriching VEGF signaling pathways, facilitating the formation of new synovial blood vessels as validated in the CIA rat model.
TAM receptors in RA-associated intestinal immune homeostasis

In healthy individuals, intestinal epithelial cells form a selective barrier through tight junction proteins, effectively containing microorganisms and their metabolites to maintain gut homeostasis. In RA, however, intestinal barrier dysfunction often precedes clinical joint manifestations, indicating its primary role in disease pathogenesis. Barrier compromise permits microbial products like LPS to enter systemic circulation via the "gut-joint axis," activating immune responses that ultimately target joint tissues and initiate clinical arthritis. This bidirectional crosstalk represents a key mechanism in RA and a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

The TAM receptor family helps maintain intestinal microbial balance and prevent immune dysregulation in RA. Clinically, TAM expression profiles correlate with gut microbiota composition: downregulation of Axl is associated with enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa (e.g., Proteobacteria, Collinsella, Eggerthella, and Prevotella copri) and depletion of beneficial genera such as Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium. These shifts are closely linked to RA disease activity. Mechanistically, TAM receptors sustain intestinal homeostasis through coordinated actions that remotely influence RA via the gut-joint axis. Axl strengthens the epithelial barrier by suppressing zonulin expression and enhancing regeneration through inhibition of the MyD88/NF-kappaB pathway. It also directly interacts with MyD88 to temper TLR4/NF-kappaB activation, preventing suppression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) including alpha-defensins and Reg3 proteins. Meanwhile, MerTK supports barrier integrity through efferocytosis of apoptotic cells, collectively limiting systemic translocation of LPS and related metabolites.

In regulating intestinal immunity, MerTK clears apoptotic neutrophils to reduce IL-1beta release and supports Paneth cell function and AMP production, while Axl induces SOCS3 expression to inhibit IFN-gamma secretion by Th1 cells. Together, these actions help prevent a pro-inflammatory intestinal milieu. TAM receptors also directly modulate microbiota composition. Gas6-activated Axl triggers the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 pathway to enhance AMP gene transcription and stimulate Paneth cell secretion, thereby restraining expansion of pro-inflammatory microbes such as P. copri and Proteobacteria and reducing release of cross-reactive autoantigens. Additionally, TAM-mediated microbial balance promotes short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production by commensal bacteria. SCFAs activate the PI3K/AKT/STAT3 pathway via FFAR2 or act as histone deacetylase inhibitors, epigenetically upregulating Axl and MerTK expression and establishing a self-reinforcing "microbiota/TAM/SCFA" axis. Notably, Axl-/- and MerTK-/- mice exhibit accumulated apoptotic neutrophils in the intestinal lamina propria and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1beta, confirming the essential role of TAM receptors in efferocytosis and inflammatory resolution in the gut. Collectively, these findings position TAM signaling as a potential biomarker and promising therapeutic target for RA and other microbiota-related inflammatory diseases.
TAM and RA-associated complications

RA is a systemic autoimmune disorder that not only causes joint damage but also affects multiple organs, leading to complications such as cardiovascular disease (CVD), pulmonary disorders, and osteoporosis (OP). TAM receptor signaling has been increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of these systemic manifestations (Fig. 5).
TAM and RA-associated complications

In cardiovascular diseases (CVD), MerTK suppresses inflammation, promotes apoptotic body clearance, and protects the heart. The role of Axl in CVD is controversial: it protects against vascular calcification but may drive renal inflammation. Tyro3 signaling protects the myocardium and prevents cardiac fibrosis. In the lungs, Axl and MerTK regulate homeostasis and inflammation; their activation improves lung diseases, though MerTK also promotes pulmonary fibrosis. In osteoporosis, MerTK and Tyro3 roles remain unclear, while Axl targets the Gas6/Axl/ERK pathway to promote osteoblast differentiation and improve bone health

In the cardiovascular system, TAM receptors play distinct and sometimes opposing roles. MerTK exerts protective effects by suppressing inflammation, promoting the resolution of inflammatory responses, and enhancing the clearance of apoptotic cells in contexts such as atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction. It facilitates the removal of dead cardiomyocytes, thereby attenuating tissue damage and fibrosis post-infarction. In contrast, the function of Axl in CVD is more complex and context-dependent. While it may protect against vascular calcification in certain settings. Axl also promotes vascular inflammation, remodeling, and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation in hypertension models. Tyro3, though less studied, appears to confer myocardial protection by inhibiting pro-fibrotic type 2 immune responses.

Within the pulmonary system, both Axl and MerTK contribute to the maintenance of lung homeostasis. They are constitutively expressed in lung cells and alveolar macrophages, where they coordinate the clearance of apoptotic cells in distinct microenvironments, Axl moderates silica-induced inflammation, while MerTK regulates the recruitment and function of neutrophils and alveolar macrophages. However, MerTK activation can also exert detrimental effects by synergizing with TGF-beta signaling to promote pulmonary fibrosis. The role of Tyro3 in lung pathology remains unclear due to its low expression and limited investigation.

Systemic bone loss leading to osteoporosis is another major complication of RA. The expression of TAM ligands is subject to hormonal regulation; for instance, estrogen downregulates Pros1 by inhibiting its promoter and upregulating miR-494, which targets Pros1 directly. Therapeutically, the Gas6/Axl pathway has emerged as a potential target for bone protection. In a postmenopausal osteoporosis model, Vildagliptin was shown to exert bone-protective effects via the Gas6/Axl/ERK5 pathway, promoting osteogenic differentiation.
TAM receptors in RA: diagnosis and treatment
Soluble TAM as biomarkers for RA diagnosis

Soluble forms of TAM receptors (sTAM), sTyro3, sAxl, and sMerTK, hold significant potential as biomarkers for evaluating disease status in RA. These soluble variants are generated through metalloproteinase-mediated cleavage of the extracellular domains of their membrane-bound counterparts and are markedly elevated in the synovial fluid of RA patients, showing promise as indicators of disease activity, severity, and prognosis. Functionally, sTAM receptors may disrupt physiological TAM signaling by acting as decoy receptors that sequester ligands such as Gas6 and Pros1, thereby attenuating downstream pathways, or by impairing essential processes including efferocytosis and platelet aggregation. Clinical studies reveal distinct expression patterns and clinical correlations for different sTAM members. Compared with OA patients, RA patients exhibit significantly higher levels of sTyro3 and sMerTK in synovial fluid, whereas sAxl and Gas6 levels show no significant difference. Systemic measurements also show increased plasma levels of sAxl and sMerTK in RA, though data on plasma sTyro3 remain limited.

The association between sTAM levels and clinical parameters further supports their biomarker utility. Zheng et al. reported significant elevations of sTyro3, sAxl, and sMerTK in RA synovial fluid, with levels strongly correlating with key clinical indicators. Wu et al. observed that while both plasma sTyro3 and sMerTK are elevated in RA, only synovial fluid sTyro3 strongly correlates with disease activity scores, underscoring its particular value for assessing joint-specific inflammation. Serum sTyro3 levels correlate positively with systemic inflammation (e.g., ESR) and radiographic bone damage, and negatively with hematological parameters such as hemoglobin, suggesting its role as a sensitive and comprehensive biomarker. Conversely, sMerTK correlates positively with disease duration and rheumatoid factor, and negatively with hemoglobin and complement levels (C3, C4). Notably, low membrane-bound Axl (mAxl) expression is associated with higher disease activity (DAS28) and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), whereas higher sAxl levels correlate with reduced immune infiltration, milder disease activity, and lower synovial cytokine expression, independent of disease stage or treatment history.
Development and progress of TAM-targeted therapeutics

Current clinical development of TAM-targeted therapies primarily focuses on small molecule inhibitors, employing two main strategic approaches: inhibition of receptor-ligand binding and suppression of kinase activity. The high structural homology within the TAM receptor kinase domains has led to the development of both selective inhibitors and multi-targeted kinase inhibitors (Table 1). While these agents are currently being evaluated primarily in oncology settings, their mechanisms of action, particularly in modulating immune responses and inflammation, suggest potential applicability to autoimmune diseases including RA.
Clinical development programmes

Approximately 20 small-molecule TAM inhibitors have entered clinical evaluation, with 15 currently in active commercial development. Bemcentinib (BGB324) represents the selective Axl inhibitor approach, demonstrating enhanced chemosensitivity and improved survival outcomes in preclinical models of resistant malignancies. MRX-2843 exemplifies the dual-inhibition strategy, targeting both MerTK and FLT3 with demonstrated efficacy in hematological malignancies and solid tumors. Sitravatinib (MGCD516) adopts a broader multi-kinase inhibition approach, targeting Axl, MerTK and other kinase receptors simultaneously. Its preclinical activity has been demonstrated in models of renal cell carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, sarcoma, and breast cancer. Current clinical investigation emphasizes combination strategies, particularly with conventional chemotherapeutics and other targeted agents. The therapeutic rationale leverages TAM receptors' established roles in mediating drug resistance, with these inhibitors positioned as potential resistance-reversal agents. Additional compounds in clinical development include cabozantinib, gilteritinib, and several investigational dual Axl/MerTK inhibitors, collectively representing a diverse pharmacological arsenal against TAM-mediated signaling pathways in human diseases.
Preclinical development programmes

Multiple novel small-molecule inhibitors targeting TAM receptors are currently under preclinical investigation, demonstrating diverse therapeutic mechanisms. NPS-1034, a dual Axl/MerTK inhibitor, exhibits anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic activities in vitro and shows synergistic effects when combined with EGFR inhibitors to overcome MET amplification-mediated resistance. LDC1267, a pan-TAM inhibitor with preferential MerTK activity, enhances NK cell-mediated tumor killing in vivo and effectively suppresses melanoma metastasis in mouse models. SGI-7079, a type II ATP-competitive inhibitor, restores erlotinib sensitivity in mesenchymal-type NSCLC independent of EGFR mutation status while concurrently inhibiting MerTK, Tyro3, and multiple other kinase targets. These emerging compounds highlight the continuing diversification of TAM-targeting strategies in preclinical development.

Conclusion

This review delineates the multifaceted roles of TAM receptors in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis, wherein Axl and MerTK primarily exert protective effects through immune homeostasis regulation and tissue preservation, while Tyro3 predominantly promotes inflammation and joint destruction. This functional dichotomy suggests distinct therapeutic strategies: targeted activation of Axl/MerTK pathways may restore immune balance, whereas Tyro3 inhibition could mitigate synovitis and bone erosion. The differential expression of soluble TAM receptors in RA patients highlights their biomarker potential, though standardized detection methods require further validation. Future therapeutic development should focus on receptor-specific modulators to overcome structural homology challenges and explore combination strategies with existing therapies. Advancing understanding of TAM signaling in specific cellular contexts and disease stages will be essential for realizing the precision therapeutic potential of this pathway in RA management.

passages.text: PathOrchestra: a comprehensive foundation model for computational pathology with over 100 diverse clinical-grade tasks

The complexity and variability of high-resolution pathological images present significant challenges in computational pathology. While AI-driven pathology foundation models have advanced the field, they require large-scale datasets, substantial storage, and significant computational resources, as well as rigorous validation for clinical applicability. We present PathOrchestra, a versatile pathology foundation model trained on 287,424 slides from 21 tissue types across three centers. Evaluated on 112 tasks from 61 private and 51 public datasets, covering digital slide preprocessing, pan-cancer classification, lesion identification, multi-cancer subtype classification, biomarker assessment, gene expression prediction, and structured report generation. Across 27,755 whole slide images and 9,415,729 region-of-interest images, it achieved over 0.950 accuracy in 47 tasks, including pan-cancer classification, lymphoma subtyping, and bladder cancer screening. It is the first to generate structured reports for colorectal cancer and lymphoma. Overall, PathOrchestra demonstrates the clinical readiness of large-scale self-supervised pathology foundation models, achieving high accuracy and offering potential to digital medicine integration.
Introduction

Pathology is heralded as the gold standard for disease diagnosis, encompassing a broad range of tasks including tumor detection, typing, grading, molecular expression analysis, prognosis assessment, and prediction of treatment response. These tasks require handling high-resolution and morphologically diverse pathological images, posing significant diagnostic resource challenges. Computational pathology (CPath) leverages powerful algorithms to interpret and quantify pathological images, providing a more precise understanding of disease mechanisms. However, traditional AI training paradigms relying on large annotated datasets face critical limitations, as accurately labeling vast pathological data across diverse disease types is often impractical, which underscores the urgent need for generalizable models that can efficiently handle multicenter data while reducing reliance on manual annotation.

The advent of self-supervised learning in computer vision (e.g., DINOv2, MoCov3, MAE) and the success of large language models like the GPT series have propelled the development of data-driven pre-training methodologies. These models leverage vast collections of whole slide images (WSIs) to learn high-quality feature representations from unlabeled data, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in downstream tasks using limited labeled data and fewer training parameters. Despite these advancements, a comprehensive evaluation of foundational pathology models is still lacking. Furthermore, the impact of pre-training data and model architecture on performance in downstream tasks remains underexplored. While technical assessments have been carried out, the clinical applicability and potential of these models remain insufficiently addressed, limiting their full integration into real-world clinical settings.
Overview of PathOrchestra.

a The foundational model was trained on 287,424 WSIs sourced from three centers, covering 21 human organs, tissues and systems. b The training strategy followed an unsupervised contrastive learning framework, utilizing a teacher model as the foundation for testing downstream tasks. c Diverse downstream task data encompasses both histology and cytology, enabling the model to support 112 clinical tasks across seven major categories. Figure c was created using the BioRender platform (biorender.com), in accordance with BioRender's academic licensing terms.
Overview of downstream tasks and dataset statistics.

It covers a total of 112 tasks, including 61 WSI tasks and 51 ROI tasks, with a vast dataset comprising 27,755 WSIs and 9,415,729 ROIs. The datasets used span both public and private sources, with 51 public datasets and 61 private datasets, incorporating over 35 types of stains and analyzing >50 genes. The downstream tasks are categorized into seven groups: Slide Preprocessing (12 tasks), Pan-Cancer (3 tasks), Lesion Identification (15 tasks), Cancer Subtyping (36 tasks), Biomarker Evaluation (36 tasks), and Gene Expression Assessment (10 tasks). The methodology employed for these tasks includes detection, retrieval, segmentation, linear classification, and weakly supervised classification approaches, utilizing models like ViTDet, KNN, Mask2Former, Linear Probing, and ABMIL.

In this paper, we present PathOrchestra (Fig. 1), a pathology foundation model that sets new performance benchmarks through a rigorous evaluation across 112 clinically relevant downstream tasks. PathOrchestra is implemented as a self-supervised vision encoder, pretrained on an extensive corpus of 287,424 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images encompassing 21 distinct tissues, organs, and systems, sourced from both proprietary archives and publicly available datasets from three independent centers. We systematically examine its translational potential in diverse clinical scenarios (Fig. 2), demonstrating robust and consistent performance on a large-scale evaluation comprising 27,755 WSIs and 9,415,729 region-of-interest (ROI) images (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). PathOrchestra achieved an accuracy exceeding 0.950 in 47 tasks, thereby establishing state-of-the-art benchmarks in real-world applications, including digital slide preprocessing, pan-cancer classification, lesion identification and detection, multi-cancer subtype classification, biomarker assessment, gene expression prediction, and structured pathology reporting.
Results
Dataset curation

The training dataset consists of 287,424 WSIs, covering 21 distinct types of tissues, organs, and systems, including Lymph Node (68,054), Stomach (59,598), Breast (32,890), Cervix (27,786), Lung (26,842), Bladder (16,326), Prostate (10,188), Kidney (9,328), Brain (7,240), Blood System (4,232), Colon (4,088), Liver (3,344), Uterus (3,086), Ovary (2,962), Skin (2,550), Head and Neck (2,526), Esophagus (2,492), Bone (1,890), Pancreas (932), Nerve (770), and Eye (300). These WSIs were digitized from frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue slides stained with H&E. The dataset consists of 268,859 WSIs derived from FFPE samples and 18,565 from frozen samples, resulting in a FFPE-to-frozen sample ratio of ~14:1. The scanning process utilized equipment from four different manufacturers, including the SQS-600P scanner (Shenzhen Shengqiang Technology Co., Ltd., China), using a 20 x objective and generating images in .sdpc format; the KF-PRO-005 scanner (Ningbo Jiangfeng Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd., China), employing a 40 x objective and producing .kfb files; the Aperio ScanScope GT 450 scanner (Aperio, USA), also using a 40 x objective to generate .svs files; and the Pannoramic MIDI II scanner (3DHISTECH, Hungary), utilizing a 40 x objective and producing .mdsx files. We sampled 256 x 256 patches at 20 x magnification, generating a total of 141,471,591 patches, all of which were used in the actual training.

The training dataset includes data from three sources, including the Xijing Hospital, Fourth Military Medical University, Xi'an, China (2023-2024) with 123,169 WSIs and 13,303 cases; The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, Hefei, China (2022-2024) with 133,999 WSIs and 16,749 cases; and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), USA (2006-2016), which encompasses contributions from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University, University of California Los Angeles (UCLA), University of Michigan, Mayo Clinic, University of Washington, and University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, totaling 30,256 WSIs and 10,990 cases. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Xijing Hospital (IRB No. KY20252335) and The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC (IRB No. 2025-RE-204) for the retrospective analysis of internal pathological images. Prior to computational analysis and model development, all internal data including WSIs and pathology reports were de-identified to ensure patient confidentiality. Since the study involved retrospective analysis of archival pathological slides without direct patient recruitment, informed consent was not required. The training data consisted solely of pathological images without any associated patient diagnoses or personal identifiers. Details were shown in Supplementary Table 4.
Pathology image preprocessing and quality control tasks

We classified the preprocessing tasks in CPath into two main categories which are pathology quality control tasks and general analysis tasks. The quality control tasks include wrinkle detection, bubble and adhesive identification, contamination detection, and blur detection. The general analysis tasks encompass pathology image identification, recognition of H&E and IHC staining, identification of IHC marker types, magnification recognition, differentiation between frozen and FFPE sections, identification of biopsy versus large specimens, and recognition of IHC membrane and nuclear positivity. Preprocessing is a critical step in the CPath workflow, directly impacting the performance of subsequent algorithms. Developing a feature extractor with strong generalization capabilities can significantly enhance model performance while reducing reliance on extensive training data and annotations. All preprocessing tasks were conducted using supervised ROI classification based on the linear probing method, with model performance evaluated using ACC and F1 scores. Detailed information on the preprocessing tasks and experimental setups is provided in the Methods section.
Performance on pathology image preprocessing and quality control tasks.

Model performance is shown for 12 region-of-interest (ROI)-level classification sub-tasks, encompassing pathology image quality assessment, magnification recognition, staining type identification, specimen collection method classification, and slide preparation form identification.

Among the 12 preprocessing-related tasks (Fig. 3), the PathOrchestra model achieved ACC and F1 scores exceeding 0.950 in 7 subtasks. The general analysis tasks demonstrated superior performance compared to the quality control tasks, with ACC and F1 scores surpassing 0.970 for pathology image identification, recognition of H&E and IHC staining, recognition of H&E and fluorescence staining, magnification discrimination, and differentiation between frozen and FFPE sections. In quality control tasks such as bubble and adhesive identification, the model achieved ACC and F1 scores above 0.980. These results demonstrate the model's robust capability to effectively execute a wide range of preprocessing tasks without extensive retraining.
Pan-cancer classification tasks

We evaluated PathOrchestra on slide-level pan-cancer classification tasks, including a 17-class pan-cancer tissue classification using an in-house FFPE dataset, a 32-class classification using data from the TCGA FFPE dataset, and a 32-class classification using data from the TCGA frozen tissue dataset. These tasks assessed the model's performance across different cancer types, data sources, and specimen preparation methods. Pan-cancer classification models are designed to recognize and distinguish multiple cancer types, necessitating strong generalization capabilities crucial for the early detection of various cancers. All tasks were performed using weakly supervised WSI classification based on the attention-based ABMIL, with model performance evaluated using AUC, ACC and F1 scores. Detailed information on these tasks and experimental setups is provided in the Methods section.
Results of pan-cancer classification tasks.

a Model performance in weakly supervised whole-slide image (WSI)-level classification tasks for 17 cancer types using in-house center data. The bar chart presents classification accuracy for each cancer type. b, c Evaluation of model performance in pan-cancer prediction for 32 high-incidence cancer types from the TCGA database across two slide formats: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and frozen sections. The bar charts display prediction accuracy for each format. Abbreviations: WSI, whole-slide image; FFPE, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded; TCGA, The Cancer Genome Atlas.

In the 17-class pan-cancer tissue classification task (Fig. 4a), the model achieved an average value for AUC of 0.988, ACC of 0.879, and F1 score of 0.863. Notably, the Prostate classification task achieved perfect scores (ACC, AUC, and F1 = 1.0). Upon inspection, all prostate samples were needle biopsies, which have consistent and visually distinctive features compared to other organ types that are mostly large surgical specimens. We speculate that this uniform sampling modality contributes to the model's strong performance in this task. For the 32-class classification using the TCGA FFPE dataset, the model attained the AUC of 0.964, ACC of 0.666, and F1 score of 0.667 (Fig. 4b). We observed that the classification performance for frozen sections was 1.4% lower in AUC, 8.9% lower in ACC, and 9% lower in F1 compared to FFPE sections under similar conditions (Fig. 4c). This discrepancy may be attributed to the better preservation of tissue structure and morphology in FFPE sections, which facilitates feature extraction and classification. These results underscore the model's robust generalization capabilities in pan-cancer classification tasks, highlighting its potential as a foundational pathology model for screening multiple cancer types and improving diagnostic accuracy.
Multi-organ lesion identification and analysis tasks

Lesion identification and detection encompass 15 tasks, including WSI-level breast cancer metastasis detection (CAMELYON16, CAMELYON17), ROI-level lymphoma tumor region segmentation (PD-L1), multi-organ tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) positive/negative screening (TCGA-TIL), breast tumor classification (PCam), colorectal malignant lesion classification (DigestPath), multi-organ cell semantic segmentation (SegPath), colorectal gland segmentation (GlaS), multi-organ nuclear instance segmentation (PanNuke), colorectal cell instance segmentation (CoNSeP), lung cancer tissue segmentation (WSSS4LUAD), cross-organ and cross-scanner adenocarcinoma segmentation (COSAS-Seg) and tissue classification (COSAS-Clas), multi-organ mitosis detection (SegPath), cervical cancer TCT inflammatory cell detection, and multi-organ PE&A inflammatory cell detection. For WSI-level classification tasks, we utilized ABMIL for weakly supervised learning, while ROI classification was evaluated using linear probing. Cell segmentation tasks were conducted using Mask2Former architectures. Classification performance was assessed using AUC, ACC and F1 scores, while segmentation performance was evaluated using mAP, CPA, IoU, and Dice coefficients. Detailed descriptions of these tasks and experimental setups are provided in the Methods section.
Cell and tissue segmentation results.

a Comparative analysis of semantic segmentation performance between PathOrchestra and UNI on the ConSeP dataset for cell segmentation. The bar chart summarizes results for three metrics-Class Pixel Accuracy (CPA), Intersection over Union (IoU), and Dice coefficient-across multiple cell types. b Performance comparison on the WSSS4LUAD dataset for tissue segmentation, evaluated across three tissue categories: tumor epithelial tissue, tumor-associated stromal tissue, and normal tissue. Results are reported for CPA, IoU, and Dice coefficient. c Representative qualitative examples of model predictions. Each pair shows the original histopathology image (left) alongside the corresponding segmentation output generated by the model (right). Abbreviations: CPA, Class Pixel Accuracy; IoU, Intersection over Union.

We evaluated the performance of PathOrchestra across multiple tasks under the multi-organ lesion identification and analysis category, with segmentation results shown in Fig. 5. For the CoNSeP task, which is a multi-organ nuclear instance segmentation task, we used three evaluation metrics: CPA, IoU, and Mean Dice. PathOrchestra performed poorly in this task, with an CPA of 0.556, IoU of 0.399, and Mean Dice of 0.550, indicating substantial room for improvement in nuclear instance segmentation. Similarly, for the WSSS4LUAD task, which is a semantic segmentation task, the CPA was 0.877, IoU was 0.771, and Mean Dice was 0.871. For the SegPath task, we segmented lesion regions in images using evaluation metrics including Precision, Recall, and Mean Dice. The experimental results showed that PathOrchestra achieved a Precision of 0.756, Recall of 0.720, and Dice of 0.717 in the SegPath task, demonstrating balanced segmentation performance and the ability to effectively identify and segment lesion regions. For the Gland segmentation task (based on the GlaS dataset), we evaluated the performance of PathOrchestra in glandular region segmentation, using Precision, Recall, and Dice as evaluation metrics. The results showed that the model achieved a Precision of 0.929, Recall of 0.868, and Dice of 0.931, indicating good performance in glandular region segmentation. For the PanNuke task, PathOrchestra achieved a Precision of 0.923, Recall of 0.833, and Dice of 0.849, demonstrating excellent performance in nuclear segmentation.

In the mitosis detection task, we also evaluated the performance of PathOrchestra under the SegPath task, using mAP (bbox, IoU = 0.5), mAP (seg, IoU = 0.5), and mAP (seg, IoU = 0.75) as evaluation metrics. The experimental results showed that the model's mAP (bbox, IoU = 0.5) and mAP (seg, IoU = 0.5) were 0.885 and 0.883, respectively, while mAP (seg, IoU = 0.75) was 0.658. These results indicate that PathOrchestra has limitations in accurately locating and segmenting mitotic cells, especially at higher segmentation precision requirements. For two cell detection tasks, namely TCT inflammatory cell detection and PE&A inflammatory cell detection, the results showed that PathOrchestra achieved an mAP (bbox, IoU = 0.5) of 0.351 in the TCT inflammatory cell detection task, while the mAP in the PE&A inflammatory cell detection task was only 0.634, indicating considerable performance variation across different cell type detection tasks.

For other classification tasks, we used ACC, F1, and AUC as evaluation metrics. PathOrchestra performed excellently in the breast cancer metastasis detection task (WSI level), achieving 1.00 for ACC, F1, and AUC on the CAMELYON16 dataset, while its performance on CAMELYON17 was subpar, with an ACC of 0.840, F1 of 0.588, and AUC of 0.784. However, on the Pcam dataset, which is also a breast cancer classification model, PathOrchestra performed well, achieving an ACC of 0.916, F1 of 0.916, and AUC of 0.975. In other classification tasks, such as lymphoma PD-L1 tumor region detection, TIL positivity detection, and DigestPath tumor cell classification, PathOrchestra's ACC values were 0.851, 0.931, and 0.916, respectively, with AUCs of 0.927, 0.959, and 0.975, demonstrating good classification performance. However, in some tasks, such as COSAS screening and COSAS tissue classification, the model's AUC values were relatively low, at 0.897 and 0.624, respectively, indicating its shortcomings in complex tissue type classification tasks. Overall, PathOrchestra demonstrated some potential in multi-organ lesion identification and analysis tasks, but improvements are still needed in certain tasks to enhance the model's accuracy and robustness, particularly in more complex segmentation and cell detection tasks.
Multi-cancer subtype classification tasks

Tumor classification and subtyping are critical in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and personalizing treatment plans, thereby optimizing patient prognosis and clinical outcomes. We evaluated the performance of PathOrchestra across tumor classification and subtyping tasks, including cervical cancer subtyping, bladder cancer screening (WSI and ROI), cervical TCT screening (WSI and ROI), gastrointestinal benign and malignant screening, lymphoma and reactive hyperplasia screening, lymphoma cell origin classification, colorectal cancer detection, cervical epithelial lesion detection, colorectal and lung tissue screening (LC25K), lung cancer subtyping (LC25K-lung), colorectal subtyping (LC25K-colon), breast cancer screening (BreastHis), lung cancer subtyping (TCGA-NSCLC), colorectal subtyping (TCGA-RCC), lymphoma subtyping, breast cancer subtyping (BACH), esophageal cancer screening (TCGA-ESCA), colorectal tissue classification (HunCRC-patch), prostate ISUP grading (PANDA), prostate Gleason grading, colorectal high and low-grade screening, gastric cancer subtyping (PatchGastricAD22), prostate cancer tissue classification (AGGC), glioma IDH1 screening (TCGA-IDH1), multi-organ lymph node metastasis screening, colorectal polyp screening, colorectal subtyping (HunCRC-WSI), renal cancer tissue classification (TCGA-RCC), colorectal tissue classification (CRC-100K), colorectal subtyping (institutional data), colorectal tissue classification (Kather), and brain subtyping (Ebrains). Detailed information on these tasks and experimental setups is provided in the Methods section.
Results of multi-cancer subtype classification.

The bar charts show PathOrchestra's performance across region-of-interest (ROI)-level (blue outlines) and whole-slide image (WSI)-level (green outlines) multi-cancer subtype classification tasks. Key performance metrics, including accuracy (ACC) and F1 score, are presented for each task. Results are compared between public and private datasets, demonstrating the model's robustness across diverse classification challenges. Each panel displays a separate classification setting, with ROI-level and WSI-level curves overlaid for direct comparison. All colors and abbreviations are defined as follows: ROI, region of interest; WSI, whole-slide image; ACC, accuracy.

In the evaluation of 34 tumor classification and subtype identification tasks (Fig. 6), PathOrchestra demonstrated broad adaptability and high performance levels. Notably, in the classification tasks for cervical and bladder cancers, PathOrchestra excelled. For instance, the ACC for benign and malignant bladder cancer classification reached 0.954, with an F1 score of 0.943 and an AUC value of 0.989, showcasing the model's exceptional performance in this task. Furthermore, in the patch classification task for bladder cancer, the model's F1 score improved to 0.945, while the ACC and AUC values also reached 0.945 and 0.988, respectively, indicating that the model maintains efficiency even in more granular image processing scenarios. In the screening for benign and malignant gastrointestinal tumors, PathOrchestra exhibited remarkable precision, achieving an ACC of 0.993, an F1 score of 0.976, and an AUC as high as 0.988. These results highlight the model's strong diagnostic potential in the detection and classification of gastrointestinal cancers. In lymphoma-related classification tasks, PathOrchestra also demonstrated robust performance. For example, in the task of classifying lymphoma versus reactive hyperplasia, the model achieved an ACC of 0.975, an F1 score of 0.941, and an AUC of 0.994. In the more refined classification of B/T-cell lymphomas, PathOrchestra recorded an F1 score of 0.918 and an AUC of 0.993, reflecting the model's high accuracy in subtype classification. Similarly, in the subtype classification tasks for colorectal and lung cancers, PathOrchestra performed admirably. In the colorectal subtype classification (LC25K-2), all evaluation metrics (ACC, F1, and AUC) achieved 1.000, demonstrating absolute classification accuracy. Likewise, for the lung cancer subtype classification (LC25K-3), the model attained a high ACC and F1 score of 0.999, with an AUC of 0.999, indicating strong generalization capabilities across different tissue types.

However, despite PathOrchestra's outstanding performance in most tasks, there are areas for improvement. For instance, in the IDH1 screening task for gliomas, although the AUC reached 0.940, the accuracy and F1 scores were relatively low at 0.896 and 0.894, suggesting that the model's precision in screening this specific subtype may not match its performance in other cancers. In more complex tasks, PathOrchestra's performance was comparatively weaker. For example, in the prostate cancer grading (AGGC) task, the model achieved an ACC of only 0.660, an F1 score of 0.828, and an AUC of 0.873, reflecting limitations in handling highly complex pathological tasks. Additionally, in glioma screening (Ebrains), although the AUC reached 0.871, the ACC and F1 scores were notably lower at 0.386 and 0.278, indicating a need for further optimization in brain tumor screening. In summary, PathOrchestra demonstrated exceptional accuracy and robustness across various cancer classification and subtype identification tasks, particularly excelling in bladder cancer, gastrointestinal cancers, and colorectal cancer tasks. Nevertheless, there remains room for improvement in certain complex tasks, such as prostate cancer grading and glioma screening. This indicates that while PathOrchestra performs excellently in most tasks, further optimization is necessary for specific tasks to enhance its overall diagnostic capability.
Biomarker assessment tasks

Biomarker evaluation is critical for clinical diagnosis, treatment selection, and prognostic assessment. We evaluated PathOrchestra across 36 biomarker-related tasks involving the qualitative assessment and scoring of commonly used IHC markers. These included over 30 protein markers with varied biological functions, expression patterns, and clinical significance. The model demonstrated robust performance across diverse markers and datasets, highlighting its adaptability to complex molecular evaluation tasks. Full task descriptions and experimental details are provided in the Methods section.

Structured report generation tasks

Generating pathology reports is one of the most challenging clinical tasks in computational pathology, primarily due to the large number of WSIs per patient, the complexity of diagnostic content, and the difficulty in predicting subtasks. By selecting appropriate disease types and breaking down the pathology report into a structured format, we can use artificial intelligence algorithms to generate pathology reports from diagnostic and auxiliary examination perspectives. This approach can effectively save time of pathologists while providing reasonable diagnostic explanations, thus holding significant value for clinical practice. This study focuses on two diseases, lymphoma and colorectal cancer, employing a subtask combination method to generate structured reports for each patient based on the PathOrchestra model.
